title: The Inconvenient Figure
body: The utilisation rate for your division's flagship scheme came in at 31%. {senior}, the {senior.title} your division answers to, asks, mildly, whether it might be "presented as a range rather than a number".

choices.text: Present it as a range.
choices.outcome: The slide reads "30-60%". Nobody asks. {senior} says nothing further about it, which you decide to read as approval.

choices.text: Present the number.
choices.outcome: The meeting runs forty minutes over. The scheme is reviewed. {senior} does not invite you to the next one, or the four after that. It is noted.

choices.text: Present the number, with a recovery plan attached.
choices.outcome: You spend the weekend on eleven slides nobody asked for. {senior} presents them as {senior.their} own. The scheme survives. So do you.

title: The Report
body: A consultancy has been engaged for $1.9 million to study the problem. Their final deck recommends, in different words, the thing you wrote in a minute paper two years ago.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them have it.
choices.outcome: The recommendation is adopted enthusiastically. At the townhall it is described as "a fresh external perspective". You clap.

choices.text: Circulate your old minute paper.
choices.outcome: The email is received in silence by fourteen people. One of them, a deputy secretary you have never met, replies only to you: "Noted. Good paper." You keep that email for years. It is noted.

choices.text: Ask the consultants, in the Q&A, what their data source was.
choices.outcome: It was you. It was your minute paper. The room enjoys this more than the partner does.

title: Public Sector Transformation
body: Two days offsite, with {peer} at your table. There are post-its. You have been asked to ideate on how the division might become "more agile, more citizen-centric, and more data-driven" without additional headcount or budget.

choices.text: Write down what everyone is actually thinking.
choices.outcome: Your post-it says "we need three more officers". {peer} puts one up beside it that says "agree". Neither appears in the deck. It is noted.

choices.text: Produce an acronym.
choices.outcome: You offer S.E.R.V.E. The facilitator writes it in green marker. It appears on a banner in the lift lobby for the next six years.

choices.text: Volunteer to write the follow-up implementation plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted it. It becomes the only document from the offsite that anyone reads, which makes it, quietly, yours.

variants.title: Design Thinking
variants.body: A design-thinking sprint. There is a journey map on the wall, a persona called "Auntie Mary", and a facilitator who has asked everyone to put their assumptions in a box on the whiteboard marked PARKING LOT.

choices.text: Park the assumption everyone actually has.
choices.outcome: You write "no new resources" on a sticky note and put it in the parking lot. The facilitator laughs, then stops laughing, then moves it to a corner. It is noted.

choices.text: Give Auntie Mary a tagline.
choices.outcome: "Auntie Mary: Served Once, Served Right." It is printed on a tote bag. You see the tote bag at hawker centres for years.

choices.text: Volunteer to turn the wall into a plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted the wall. Your plan is the only thing from the sprint that survives the sprint, which makes it, quietly, yours.

variants.title: The Retreat
variants.body: A transformation retreat at a hotel on Sentosa. The breakout rooms are named after the organisation's values. You have been assigned to Integrity, which is the room with no window.

choices.text: Say, in Integrity, what the room is for.
choices.outcome: You say the division needs three more officers, not a fourth value. The room agrees in silence. The scribe does not write it down. It is noted.

choices.text: Coin a value.
choices.outcome: You propose "Ownership with Heart". It is adopted by the afternoon and on a lanyard by the end of the quarter.

choices.text: Volunteer to write up the retreat.
choices.outcome: You write it up properly, with owners and dates. It is the only retreat report anyone has ever acted on, and you are now, somehow, in charge of it.

variants.body: A scenario-planning day: four futures for Singapore in 2060, laid out on a two-by-two matrix, and a facilitator's rule that nobody may say "budget" before lunch. Every future, you notice, has your division in it, unchanged.

choices.text: Say "budget" at 11:15.
choices.outcome: You point out that all four futures assume today's headcount. The facilitator writes "resourcing" outside the matrix, in a corner that belongs to no future at all. It is noted.

choices.text: Give the four futures names.
choices.outcome: You call them Harbour, Haze, Heartland and Hive. The names outlive the exercise by a decade. Hive turns up, years later, in a Minister's speech, meaning something else.

choices.text: Volunteer to write up the implications.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted the implications. Your paper turns four futures into six actions with owners and dates. Two of them happen within the year: the only part of 2060 to arrive early.

variants.title: The Innovation Challenge
variants.body: The division's innovation challenge: five teams, five-minute pitches, a panel of three directors and a $5,000 grant for a prototype. Your team's idea is good. The team before yours has a logo.

choices.text: Pitch the real problem: there are not enough of you.
choices.outcome: Your five minutes are about headcount. The panel thanks you for your candour and gives the grant to the logo. Your slide turns up, unattributed, at the next directors' retreat. It is noted.

choices.text: Give your idea a logo, and an acronym.
choices.outcome: Your idea becomes S.P.A.R.K. It wins by one vote. The panel's chair presents the cheque and asks what it stands for, and nobody on your team can remember.

choices.text: Offer to build the winning idea, whoever's it is.
choices.outcome: The logo wins. Its owners move on to next year's challenge, and you build their idea over the following year, quietly. Version two, the one that ships, is yours.

title: A Word You Have Not Heard Before
body: Over lunch, a friend in HR mentions your CEP. You ask what that is. There is a pause of exactly the wrong length, and then a change of subject.

choices.text: Press her on it.
choices.outcome: Currently Estimated Potential. The highest grade the service thinks you will ever reach. It is decided about you, reviewed without you, and never disclosed to you. You think about this in the lift, and then most days after that.

choices.text: Let it go.
choices.outcome: You let it go. You will hear the term again, years from now, in a sentence that begins "well, realistically".

title: The Nomination
body: One name from your division goes forward for the Public Service Leadership Programme this year. {senior}, who signs off on nominations, asks for yours by Friday. It may be your own. Everyone expects it to be the obvious scholar's.

choices.text: Nominate yourself.
choices.outcome: It is not done, saying it out loud. It is also not forbidden. {senior} writes your name down slowly, and a committee you will never meet revises your CEP upward.

choices.text: Nominate the obvious scholar.
choices.outcome: He was going anyway. He thanks you warmly and genuinely, which is somehow worse, and the officer who does the actual work reads the shortlist on the intranet, like everyone else.

choices.text: Nominate the quiet officer who does all the actual work.
choices.outcome: She is astonished. She goes, and for nine months her work lands on your desk. She rises faster than you do, and never once forgets who put her name in.

title: Oil at East Coast
body: At 4:10am on a Saturday, a bunker tanker is holed off the Southern Islands. By Monday there is oil on the beach at East Coast, four agencies, a task force, and a 6pm press conference with no holding statement.

choices.text: Take the pen: write the 6pm statement.
choices.outcome: Eleven drafts. The Minister reads the ninth almost word for word, down to the metres of boom laid. On Tuesday the transcript goes round the ministries with one line added: who wrote it.

choices.text: Take the ops room: booms, beaches, rosters.
choices.outcome: Nine days of booms, shovels, contractors and volunteers who bring their own buckets. The oil gets no further than East Coast. Nobody outside the room ever knows how close it came.

choices.text: Stay at your own desk. It is not your division.
choices.outcome: It was not your division. When the task force stands down, its thank-you lunch has forty-one names on the list. You know every one of them.

variants.title: The Siren
variants.body: At 4:10am on a Saturday, every Public Warning System siren on the island sounds the Important Message signal. There is no message. By Monday there are three ministries, a task force, and a 6pm press conference to explain nothing.

choices.text: Take the pen: explain, at 6pm, that nothing happened.
choices.outcome: Nine drafts on how to say that nothing happened without sounding as if something did. The last is read out at 6pm, and calms an island. On Tuesday three Permanent Secretaries ask who wrote it.

choices.text: Take the ops room: the hotline, the vendor, every siren.
choices.outcome: Nine days on the hotline and with the vendor, then every siren on the island, checked by hand. None sounds out of turn again. That was the job, and it leaves no trace.

choices.text: Go back to bed. It is not your division.
choices.outcome: It was not your division. By Wednesday everyone on your floor can explain the Important Message signal, and does, at length. You were awake at 4:10am as well. Nobody counts that.

variants.title: Lights Out
variants.body: At 7:40pm on a Thursday, a substation fault blacks out a third of the island for forty minutes, stopping lifts and trains where they stand. By morning there are three ministries, a task force, and a 6pm press conference.

choices.text: Take the pen: the 6pm statement, and the apology in it.
choices.outcome: Eleven drafts, the last four about a single word, "regret". The Minister keeps it. On Friday the Head of Civil Service asks who chose the word, and is told, and writes your name down.

choices.text: Take the ops room: lifts first, then everything else.
choices.outcome: You run the room through the night: two hundred lift rescues, each one logged, none of them late. By morning the grid is back and the log is in order. Nobody reads the log.

choices.text: Go home, by the stairs. It is not your division.
choices.outcome: It was not your division. You were, however, in a lift at 7:40pm, for thirty-one minutes, and you are the only person in the building who never mentions it.

title: The Forum Page
body: A member of the public has written to the Straits Times Forum page about a scheme your division runs. His letter is 340 words long, very angry, and right about every fact. {senior} wants the ministry's reply drafted by Friday, and the paper will print whatever goes out.

choices.text: Draft the standard reply: thank him for his feedback.
choices.outcome: Your reply says the scheme "is regularly reviewed", in 310 words that commit to nothing. It's approved in a single round, which tells you exactly what gets approved easily here.

choices.text: Draft a reply that admits he's right, and says what will change.
choices.outcome: It goes through nine rounds of approval and comes out shorter, but the admission survives. He writes in again, to thank you. That letter doesn't get published.

choices.text: Look him up in the ministry's records first.
choices.outcome: He's a retired schoolteacher in Ang Mo Kio. You close the window without doing anything with it. But you did open his file, and the system logs who opens what.

title: The Posting
body: Three years in Washington, or Beijing, or Brussels. It is a good posting. Your daughter is nine and has just settled into a school she loves.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Three good years. You come back with a network, a much better sense of how small the country is, and a daughter who has stopped mentioning her old school.

choices.text: Turn it down.
choices.outcome: "Family reasons" is accepted immediately, warmly, and with complete understanding, and it is written down.

choices.text: Ask for it to be deferred two years.
choices.outcome: It is deferred. It is not re-offered. Nobody ever tells you that it will not be re-offered; you simply notice, eventually, that it has not been.

title: The Tender
body: The evaluation has the vendors 0.3 points apart. The stronger proposal is from a firm whose director left your ministry eighteen months ago and still sends you a Chinese New Year card. This year's came the week the tender closed.

choices.text: Award it. The proposal genuinely is better.
choices.outcome: It genuinely is better, and you write four pages saying why, which is three more than anyone writes for a vendor they have never met. The card goes in the file too. Files are kept.

choices.text: Recuse yourself from the evaluation.
choices.outcome: The panel picks the same firm without you, and your project goes to someone who was not in the room. Your recusal memo is the best thing in the file.

choices.text: Award it to the other vendor to be safe.
choices.outcome: The other vendor wins, on a score you had to adjust twice. The project runs eleven months late. You were not wrong to worry about perception; you were wrong to let it decide.

title: Meet-the-People Session
body: An old school friend volunteers at her MP's Meet-the-People Session and asks you to help on Tuesday nights, writing appeal letters to agencies for residents. Most of the cases were decided correctly the first time. The sessions are run by the party's branch, and civil servants are meant to stay out of politics. She says lots of people help in their own time.

choices.text: Go every Tuesday for a year, in your own time.
choices.outcome: Fifty-one Tuesdays, in your own T-shirt, never the branch one. You learn more about how policy lands than in all your years of writing it. One appeal you argue properly, for a woman everyone said was hopeless, wins. The MP notices.

choices.text: Go a few times, enough to be seen.
choices.outcome: You go four times, and make sure the MP sees you on two of them. You learn very little about how policy lands. The branch learns that you are interested.

choices.text: Decline. You are a civil servant, and mean to stay neutral.
choices.outcome: Your friend says she completely understands. The branch secretary, standing next to her, also understands, and will remember your name if it ever comes up.

title: The Officer You Are Supervising
body: He is twenty-six, extremely clever, on the Administrative Service, and will outrank you in about four years. He has asked you to review his paper. It is not good.

choices.text: Tell him plainly, and teach him.
choices.outcome: He takes it well, rewrites it twice, and becomes rather good. He will outrank you soon, and he will remember.

choices.text: Clear it. Let him find out the hard way.
choices.outcome: He presents it. It goes badly. He is moved to a better posting three months later anyway, which teaches him a different lesson than the one you intended.

choices.text: Rewrite it yourself overnight.
choices.outcome: It is now a good paper with his name on it. He thanks you. He does not learn to write, and he does not need to.

title: The Leak
body: A policy under discussion has appeared, in accurate detail, on a Telegram channel. The circulation list was eleven people. You are one of them.

choices.text: Cooperate fully with the internal inquiry.
choices.outcome: It takes four months. It concludes that the source could not be determined. The eleven of you are never quite the same with each other again.

choices.text: Quietly work out who it was. Tell no one.
choices.outcome: It takes a fortnight. It was {peer}, from your own intake, for a reason you find you have some sympathy with. You keep it, and {peer} never learns that you know.

choices.text: It was you.
choices.outcome: It was you, and you had what you still believe were good reasons. The inquiry does not find you. You wait years to find out whether that holds.

title: The Pingat
body: Your name is on this year's National Day Awards list. The medal is the entry-level one, but it is a state honour, presented at an investiture, and your family will be extremely proud without understanding which one it is. Your team, who did much of the work behind it, are not on the list.

choices.text: Accept, and bring your family to the investiture.
choices.outcome: Your family dresses as if for a wedding and photographs everything, including the carpet. You realise afterwards that it was the best day they have had in years, and it cost you nothing.

choices.text: Accept, and ask that your team be recognised too.
choices.outcome: You are told this year's list is fixed. So at the division meeting you give the medal's mention entirely to your team. A mention is not a medal, everyone knows it, and it still lands.

title: Lo Hei
body: It's the division's Chinese New Year lunch, and the Permanent Secretary is at your table. After eleven minutes of tossing yusheng and shouting good wishes, she turns to you and asks, properly: "So, what do you actually think we're getting wrong?"

choices.text: Tell her, specifically, with an example.
choices.outcome: You have about ninety seconds, and you use all of them. She stops eating to listen. At the end she says, "Say that again on Thursday, to the committee." The people who decide promotions will be in that room.

choices.text: Say something safe about communications.
choices.outcome: "Mm," she says, and turns to the person on her left. That's the end of it, and you both know it.

choices.text: Turn the question back to her.
choices.outcome: She answers it at length, and very well. You learn a great deal. She learns nothing about you, which is what she was asking.

title: The Inter-Ministry Committee
body: An IMC has been convened. It has met eleven times. Its interim finding is that further study is warranted. You are the secretariat.

choices.text: Write a paper that forces a decision.
choices.outcome: Your paper presents three options and recommends one. Two ministries object. A decision is made anyway, largely to stop the paper circulating. It is noted.

choices.text: Keep taking excellent minutes.
choices.outcome: Your minutes are widely admired. The committee meets fourteen more times. You are commended for your support of the committee's work.

choices.text: Leak the deadlock to {journalist}, a friendly {journalist.title}.
choices.outcome: A decision follows within a month. You had been right about what needed to happen and wrong about how, and only one of those is survivable.

title: The Ballot
body: Fourth BTO application. Non-mature estate, four-room. At work you are, technically, the government.

choices.text: Ballot again like everyone else.
choices.outcome: Queue number 2,847 of 610 units. You laugh in the lift. At the next family dinner you are noticeably better at explaining the scheme, because now you have also lost.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB whether anything is coming up.
choices.outcome: There is nothing improper in what he tells you — it is all public, three weeks early. That is the whole of the impropriety, and you both know its exact size.

choices.text: Buy resale. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done by Thursday. The cash-over-valuation hurts for eleven years, and you never again have to explain a queue number at a family dinner.

variants.title: The Prime Launch
variants.body: This launch is a Prime project: a central location, a lower price now, a clawback of the subsidy when you sell, and a minimum occupation period of ten years. The queue is already longer than the estate.

choices.text: Apply, and take your chances.
choices.outcome: Queue number 1,206 for 290 units. You do the arithmetic once, and then decide not to do it again.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB how the next launch looks.
choices.outcome: He tells you which launch next quarter will have the shorter queue. It is on the website three weeks later, word for word. For three weeks, you were the website.

choices.text: Buy resale instead, and stop thinking about it.
choices.outcome: You buy a 1990s five-room with its original kitchen cabinets and a view of a multi-storey carpark. The loan is long. The cabinets are, it turns out, very good.

variants.title: The Fifth Ballot
variants.body: Fifth application. The ballot results page now remembers you. Your queue numbers, laid end to end, would house a small town.

choices.text: Ballot again.
choices.outcome: Queue number 3,104. You screenshot it for a group chat that has become, over five years, mainly a support group.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB what is coming up.
choices.outcome: He walks you through next quarter's launches over kopi. Every word of it goes on the website three weeks later. You have, technically, only had your kopi early.

choices.text: Buy resale. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done in a week. The valuation comes in below the price, and the difference has to be paid in cash, which is the rule and is also most of your savings.

title: Committee of Supply
body: The COS cuts. Your Minister has eight minutes and needs one announceable thing. Your division has nothing ready, and nobody in the room wants to be the one who says so.

choices.text: Announce the pilot you have been quietly building.
choices.outcome: It is eighteen months from ready. It is announced as though it is four. You spend the next eighteen months making the announcement retroactively true, and you manage it, mostly.

choices.text: Rebrand an existing scheme with a new name and a higher number.
choices.outcome: "Enhanced". It is enhanced by the word "enhanced". It is covered favourably. Nobody is harmed and nothing is gained and this is, you suspect, most of what happens here.

choices.text: Tell the Minister there is nothing, and say so early.
choices.outcome: He is annoyed for a day and grateful for a year, because the alternative was being annoyed in Parliament. He does not forget either part. It is noted.

variants.title: Paragraph 14
variants.body: The draft of the Minister's Committee of Supply speech has a gap at paragraph 14, marked [ANNOUNCEMENT: DIVISION TO PROVIDE]. Your division is the division. The draft goes to him on Friday.

choices.text: Fill paragraph 14 with the pilot you have been building.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 14 promises it "from next year". It needs two. You spend both making paragraph 14 true, and in the end Hansard is right, a little late.

choices.text: Fill it with an old scheme, renamed and Enhanced.
choices.outcome: Paragraph 14 introduces the Enhanced scheme: the old one, with a larger number in front of it. It reads well. Nothing changes, and it is reported as a change.

choices.text: Send paragraph 14 back empty, with a note saying why.
choices.outcome: He reads the note on Friday, is irritated all weekend, and on Monday cuts paragraph 14. The speech runs a minute shorter. He remembers which minute.

variants.title: The Rehearsal
variants.body: The Minister rehearses his Committee of Supply speech aloud in the boardroom, with the press secretary timing him. At your division's page he stops, reads it twice, and asks the room what, exactly, is new.

choices.text: Answer with the pilot, though it is not ready.
choices.outcome: You describe the pilot as rather further along than it is. He likes it, and it is in the speech by evening. The next two years are spent catching up with that evening.

choices.text: Answer with an old scheme, newly Enhanced.
choices.outcome: "An Enhanced scheme, Minister." The press secretary writes it down. The coverage is warm and calls it new. Apart from its name, nothing about it is.

choices.text: Answer that nothing is, and that nothing should be dressed up.
choices.outcome: The room goes very still. He finishes the rehearsal without your page, thanks everyone, and leaves without looking at you. On the day he speaks for seven minutes, not eight.

title: The Reorganisation
body: Your division is being moved to another ministry. The rationale runs to forty slides, nobody was consulted, and the new org chart has one fewer director-level box. The two people in line for it are you and {peer}.

choices.text: Fight for your people's postings first.
choices.outcome: You place all nine of them before you place yourself, and {peer} gets the good box. The nine know exactly what you did, and one of them will be in a position to repay it.

choices.text: Secure the good box for yourself first.
choices.outcome: You get it, a week before {peer} would have. The nine are placed adequately, and something in the division's manner toward you changes in a way that is never once spoken aloud.

choices.text: Volunteer to run the transition.
choices.outcome: Nine months of thankless plumbing. It goes unusually smoothly, which means nobody notices, except the two people whose opinion of you decides your next five years.

title: The Engagement Exercise
body: A national conversation. Eleven hundred citizens across forty sessions. You are writing the synthesis report. The feedback is overwhelmingly about cost of living and it does not fit the three pillars the report was designed around.

choices.text: Add a fourth pillar.
choices.outcome: The design is spoiled and the report is true. It is published with the fourth pillar looking slightly bolted on, because it was, because it had to be.

choices.text: Distribute the feedback across the three existing pillars.
choices.outcome: It fits beautifully. The launch is well received. Somewhere in a file there is a spreadsheet of what eleven hundred people actually said, and it is not the report.

choices.text: Publish the raw feedback alongside the report.
choices.outcome: This has not been done before. It is permitted, eventually, after a fortnight of anxiety at three levels. It is the single most-read government document of the year. It is noted.

title: The New Reporting Officer
body: Your reporting officer has moved on. The new one arrives from a different ministry, knows nothing about you, and has brought two people she trusts from her old division.

choices.text: Make yourself indispensable on the hardest file.
choices.outcome: It takes eight months and it works. She is a better RO than the last one and rates you honestly, which is the first time that has happened.

choices.text: Be useful to her two people.
choices.outcome: You become the one who knows where things are. It is a real position and a small one, and you hold it for four years.

choices.text: Keep your head down until she leaves.
choices.outcome: She stays five years. Your appraisals during that period are a flat line that will be visible to every promotion board for the rest of your career.

variants.title: Standing Up
variants.body: Your reporting officer has moved on. The new one comes from the SAF after twenty-two years in uniform, holds the morning meeting standing up, and has asked two officers he once commanded to come across with him.

choices.text: Take the file nobody has briefed him on.
choices.outcome: The file turns out to hold the legal opinion. You brief him in nine minutes, standing. From then on he asks for you by surname. In his vocabulary, that is a commendation.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to his two officers.
choices.outcome: They know him; you know the building. By Christmas you are the fourth chair at their lunch table, and you keep the chair for four years. It is near the window.

choices.text: Stand easy until he moves on.
choices.outcome: His two-year stint is extended twice. Your appraisals for those six years read like a parade state: present, correct, in line, and visible to every promotion board after it.

variants.title: The Deck
variants.body: Your reporting officer has moved on. The new one is a mid-career hire from a consulting firm, calls the work "the portfolio", has brought two former colleagues in on contract, and would like everything as a deck.

choices.text: Take the file that will not fit on a slide.
choices.outcome: The file is the statutory one: an Act, two amendments and a court case. You walk her through it in an afternoon. She is quick, and from then on rates you on what you know.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to her two consultants.
choices.outcome: They need someone who knows how a clearance really moves, and you do. They bill for it. Their final report thanks you in a footnote, as a key stakeholder.

choices.text: Wait for her to go back to the private sector.
choices.outcome: She stays nine years, and likes it. In that time your appraisals do not move by a word, and every promotion board after reads the nine identical years as one.

title: The Secondment
body: A two-year secondment to a statutory board that is, everyone agrees, in some difficulty. It is not a promotion. It is either a proving ground or a siding, and nobody will tell you which.

choices.text: Go, and fix it.
choices.outcome: It was a proving ground. You find out which it was only by how the phone starts ringing in month twenty-two.

choices.text: Go, and keep your head down for two years.
choices.outcome: It becomes a siding. Sidings are not assigned; they are accepted.

choices.text: Refuse it and stay where you are visible.
choices.outcome: You stay visible doing work of no consequence, which turns out to be a worse place to be seen than a hard job nobody watched.

title: The Adviser Suggests Something
body: After a community event, the constituency's grassroots adviser stops you at the lift lobby to say you handle yourself well with people. He says it to nobody else that evening. Everyone knows what this is: the first, deniable step in finding people the party might one day field at an election. Whatever you say back will be passed on.

choices.text: Say you have thought about it.
choices.outcome: You have not said yes to anything. You have said the one sentence that puts your name on the party's list of people to watch, and the adviser will be in touch.

choices.text: Laugh it off.
choices.outcome: He laughs too, and the subject closes. He does not raise it again, and for a long time nobody from the party does either.

title: The Figure, Again

options.text: the part where you were asked

body: An audit of the scheme has requested the original utilisation data for the year you presented as a range. The request is routine. It is addressed to you by name.

choices.text: Provide everything. Explain the presentation decision.
choices.outcome: You write it down plainly, including {asked}. It is accepted with a coolness that lasts about two years and then, oddly, becomes a kind of respect.

choices.text: Provide the range, and say the raw file was not retained.
choices.outcome: The file was retained. It is retained in three places. You have now told an auditor something untrue in writing, which is a different category of thing from what you did years ago.

title: Questions About the Tender
body: A parliamentary question has been filed about procurement from firms with former public-sector directors. Your award is one of fourteen in the annex.

choices.text: Your documentation was meticulous. Let it speak.
choices.outcome: It is meticulous. The PQ is answered in eleven lines and the annex is never discussed. The care you took at the time was the entire defence, and you took it because you knew you would need it.

choices.text: Ask a friend to keep your award out of the annex.
choices.outcome: It stays out. Two people now know why it stayed out, and one of them is not you.

title: A Journalist Has Been Asking

options.text: {journalist} rings, without naming you or anyone, to say that a colleague at another paper is reconstructing an old story from the people on a circulation list years ago. The colleague has your number.
{journalist}, {journalist.aTitle}, is reconstructing an old story and has been calling people who were on a circulation list years ago. {journalist.formal} has now called you.
Someone is reconstructing an old story and has been calling people who were on a circulation list years ago. They have now called you.

body: {caller}

choices.text: Decline to comment. Say nothing to anyone.
choices.outcome: The story runs without you in it, this time. You spend a fortnight discovering exactly how much of your composure was borrowed against never being asked.

choices.text: Go to the most senior person you answer to, and tell them everything first, yourself.
choices.outcome: It is the worst forty minutes of your career and it ends the matter permanently. You are thanked for coming forward. It is meant, and it is also never forgotten.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Deputy Secretary now. She has been asked for names for a post that is, everyone understands, the last rung before the very top.

choices.text: Let her decide without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She puts your name in. She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you, because the whole point of the thing was that it was not a transaction, and it stays one by not being named.

choices.text: Tell her, before she decides, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She puts your name in anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Deputy Secretary now, several rungs above you, and she has a post to fill in her division. She asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you. She simply gives you the hardest file in the division and reads your work twice.

choices.text: Tell her, first, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She asks for you anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Permanent Secretary now, younger than you and faster. She has been asked for names for a Permanent Secretary post, which everyone understands is the last rung there is.

choices.text: Let her decide without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She puts your name in. She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you, because the whole point of the thing was that it was not a transaction.

choices.text: Tell her, before she decides, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She puts your name in anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Permanent Secretary now too, and the two of you sit on the same committees. She has been asked, quietly, which of her colleagues might one day be invited to tea.

choices.text: Let her answer without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She gives one name. You find out which only by the way certain people start greeting you in lifts.

choices.text: Tell her, before she answers, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She gives your name anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: Years ago you nominated the quiet officer who did all the actual work for the leadership programme, instead of the obvious scholar. She is a Permanent Secretary now. From time to time the Prime Minister's office asks Permanent Secretaries for a frank view of the politicians they work with, before deciding who goes up. She has been asked about you.

choices.text: Let her give it without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She gives it, and you never see it. At the next reshuffle the commentary calls you someone the civil service rates. That is the one review a politician never gets to read, and it helps.

choices.text: Tell her, before she is asked, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows, and gives her honest view anyway. It is how you finally learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is your Deputy Secretary now. At the end of a routine meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he has put your name forward for something and that he did it on the strength of one afternoon, years ago. You go back to your desk and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is a Deputy Secretary too now, on your corridor, at an age you will not ask about. At the end of a joint meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he has put your name forward for something, on the strength of one afternoon, years ago. You go back to your office and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is one of your Deputy Secretaries now. At the end of a routine meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he tells his own officers the same things now, in the same words, and that they dislike it as much as he did. He says it as though this were the point. It was.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: Years ago, the young scholar you were supervising asked you to review his paper, and you told him plainly that it was bad. He is a Permanent Secretary now. After briefing a group of MPs on a bill, he waits until the room has emptied and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he will return the favour and tell you when your speeches are bad. He does, often. They get better, and the newspapers notice before the party does.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, and says that is why he now writes your briefs himself. They are very good. They are also eleven pages long, and he expects you to read all of them.

title: An Invitation to Tea
body: An email invites you to tea. The sender's title is not explained and there is no agenda, but everyone in the country knows what this is: the party is sounding you out as a candidate for the next general election. Go, and your whole career will be looked at. Decline, and you stay a civil servant, and the invitation never comes again.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Tea is served, and the conversation is about nothing for forty minutes. Then a second man arrives with a folder: everything in your career that could embarrass the party. He opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You write three sentences and delete two of them. The reply thanks you for your candour. You will not be asked again, and you will think about this for the rest of your life.

variants.body: A phone call: a warm, unhurried voice, with no surname, asks if you are free for lunch on Thursday. You are suddenly very free. This is how the party sounds out people it might field at the next general election. Go, and they will look closely at your past. Say no, and nobody calls again.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Lunch is at a club with carpet so thick it swallows footsteps, and the talk is about nothing for an hour. Then the coffee comes, and so does a second man, with a folder on your career. He opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You say you are honoured, but committed to the service. The voice says it understands completely. It is the most understanding voice you will ever hear, and you never hear it again.

variants.body: A hand-delivered envelope on your desk asks whether you might spare an hour for a conversation "about the future". It does not say whose. It does not need to: this is the party's first approach to someone it may field at the next election. Accept, and your past will be examined. Decline, and the future goes ahead without you.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: The hour is in a quiet room with very good chairs. Two people ask for your views on the country. Then the older man, without changing his tone, opens a folder on your career and begins to read from it.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You reply by hand, because it seems right, and say no. A handwritten thank-you arrives within a day. Then the future happens, without you in it.

title: The Background Check
body: Before the party puts you up for election, it checks everything that could come out in a campaign. The man from the tea is back with the same folder. Whatever you admit counts against you, and admit too much and the invitation quietly lapses. Whatever you hide may surface during the campaign. He does not say which parts he means.

choices.text: Disclose everything, including the things they may not have.
choices.outcome: He listens without writing anything until you have finished, then writes for a long time. Whatever happens next, nothing in that folder can surprise you on the campaign trail.

choices.text: Answer exactly what is asked and nothing more.
choices.outcome: The questions are precise and so are your answers. He thanks you. Nobody mentions the folder again, so you know it is still there, and that anything in it can still come out.

variants.body: The background check, in a room with a window that does not open. Before fielding you, the party must know what could come out in a campaign. The man from the tea asks; a colleague writes. Your folder lies between them, closed. Somehow that is worse. Admit too much and the invitation lapses. Hide something and it may surface later.

choices.text: Tell them everything, including what is not in the folder.
choices.outcome: You talk for forty minutes and the colleague fills four pages. At the end the man says, "Thank you. That was very complete." It sounds like the highest praise either of them is allowed to give.

choices.text: Answer the questions you are asked, and only those.
choices.outcome: Precise questions, precise answers, and nobody opens the folder. When you leave it is still on the table, closed. It will be opened again later, somewhere else, perhaps by a journalist.

variants.body: The party's background check starts as a form: forty-two questions, three about companies you have never heard of and one about a company you have. Then a meeting with the man from the tea, to "go through it together". What you admit now costs you, and too much ends the invitation. What you leave out may come out in the campaign.

choices.text: Go through all of it, including question thirty-one.
choices.outcome: You go through everything, and then the things the form did not ask. The meeting runs an hour over. Nobody seems to mind; that appears to have been the point.

choices.text: Go through what is on the form.
choices.outcome: Every question is answered completely and exactly. Question thirty-one is answered in eleven words. The meeting ends on time, and the folder goes back into a drawer you do not get to see.

title: The General Election
body: The party is fielding you at the general election, so you have resigned from the service to stand. Lose, and your career ends here. You can run in a GRC as one of a team of five, the safer choice, or alone in a single seat: riskier, and entirely yours. Then come nine days of walkabouts in relentless heat.

choices.text: Run in the GRC. Ride the team.
choices.outcome: Your name is fourth on the poster. You shake eleven thousand hands and understand, with total clarity, that almost none of this is about you.

choices.text: Ask for the single seat.
choices.outcome: A contested single seat, alone, against a decent opponent with a real ground game. Nobody carries you, and if it goes wrong, there is nobody else to blame.

variants.body: Polling Day is announced on a Monday, and the party names you as a candidate. You have resigned from the service to stand, so losing ends your career. A GRC team shares the risk and the credit; a single seat is yours alone, win or lose. By Wednesday your face is on a lamp post, and the coffee shop under it has opinions.

choices.text: Stand in the GRC, with the team.
choices.outcome: You spend nine days learning which blocks have lifts that stop on every floor. The anchor minister does the rally speeches. You do the lifts.

choices.text: Ask for the single-member seat.
choices.outcome: A single seat, a real opponent, and nobody to share the swing with. Yours is the only name on your posters. It is thrilling for exactly one day.

variants.body: The party's candidates are photographed in a school hall that smells of floor polish. You have left the service to stand, and if you lose there is no way back. Across the hall, a candidate you once sat beside at a seminar is being photographed for the other side, and waves. The party asks where you will stand: with a GRC team, or alone.

choices.text: Stand with the team in the GRC.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts in a team of five. At every coffee shop someone asks which one you are. By the end of the campaign, you can answer.

choices.text: Ask for the single seat.
choices.outcome: Nine days of being the only candidate anyone in the ward asks for. By the last rally your voice has gone and your opponent's has not. It feels significant, and is not.

title: The Maiden Speech
body: Your maiden speech, your first in Parliament, falls on day three of the debate on the President's Address. It will tell the House, the press and the Whip what kind of Member you mean to be, and it cannot be taken back. Nineteen Members spoke on day one, so the House is tired. You have three drafts.

choices.text: The draft about your ward.
choices.outcome: Lifts, hawkers and a void deck with a chess table. Three colleagues call it lovely in the lift, and your residents cut it out of the newsletter. Theirs is the only review that votes.

choices.text: The draft about the one thing from the service you believe.
choices.outcome: It is quoted, and two of the quotations are the lines you meant. A Minister you have never met sends a note: "That needed saying." The Whip sends a longer note, about what government backbenchers say in public.

choices.text: The draft praising the policy you used to doubt.
choices.outcome: Fluent, generous and on message. The Minister responsible nods twice. In your old ministry, an officer who sat through your objections for years reads it in Hansard and forwards it on without comment.

variants.body: Day three of the debate on the President's Address: you rise at 4:40pm, after a Minister and before the break, to give your maiden speech. A first speech sets how the party and the press see you for years, and the Whip will read every line. On your phone are three versions, all finished.

choices.text: Give the version about your ward.
choices.outcome: Eleven minutes on your blocks, your hawkers and the chess table at a void deck. It is warm, local and over before the break. Your ward's newsletter prints it in full.

choices.text: Give the version with the thing you believe.
choices.outcome: Eleven minutes on what you believed in the service and could never say there. The House goes quiet, the good kind. Afterwards the Whip's note to you is longer than your best line.

choices.text: Give the version praising the policy you once doubted.
choices.outcome: Generous and on message. The Minister responsible thanks you by name in the wrap-up. Your old colleagues, who heard your doubts for years, read it in Hansard and say nothing.

variants.body: Your maiden speech, your first in the House, is next week. The Whip's office has sent guidance on length, guidance on tone, and a sample first line: "I rise in support of the motion." The speech tells the party what kind of Member you will be. You have kept the first line. The rest is up to you.

choices.text: Write the rest about your ward.
choices.outcome: The rest is about your ward, and it is good. A resident posts the Hansard link in the block's WhatsApp group with the caption "our one". You keep a screenshot.

choices.text: Write the rest about what you believe.
choices.outcome: The rest is the thing you believed in the service and never said. It is quoted, mostly correctly. The Whip's office sends further guidance, this time addressed to you alone.

choices.text: Write the rest in the same spirit, and keep your doubts.
choices.outcome: Nineteen minutes in support of the motion, with your doubts kept for later. The Whip's office uses your speech as next year's sample: the first line, and all the rest.

title: The Town Council
body: Lift C at Blk 77 has broken down nine times this year, and your Town Council must decide what to do. A proper replacement means a tender, which takes five months. {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}, knows a contractor who could start on Monday if the tender is waived. Waivers are allowed in an emergency, and auditors read every one.

choices.text: Tender it properly, and explain the delay.
choices.outcome: Five months of complaints at every Tuesday session. The new lift comes in on budget from the lowest compliant bid. Years later the auditors read the file and find nothing to say.

choices.text: Waive the tender. Call {grassroots}'s contractor.
choices.outcome: The lift runs again in eleven weeks and the block is delighted. The waiver's justification is two lines long. The Town Councils Financial Rules expect more, and so, one day, will an auditor.

choices.text: Have the term contractor patch it while the tender runs.
choices.outcome: The term contractor patches Lift C six times in five months, at a cost the finance committee reads out slowly. The new lift arrives on budget, and the patches are minuted separately.

variants.body: Blk 77's lift keeps breaking down, and the Town Council meets to decide on a new one. The managing agent's slide has three options. The third, circled in pen, comes from {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}: a firm that could start on Monday, without a tender. Skipping a tender is allowed in an emergency, and auditors check every time it happens. Every head turns to you.

choices.text: Choose the tender, and minute why.
choices.outcome: The minutes record why, in a paragraph you dictate yourself. {grassroots} votes with you and does not speak to you at the tea break. The lift is replaced in five months.

choices.text: Choose the circled option, as an emergency.
choices.outcome: The firm starts on Monday and finishes in eleven weeks. The minutes say "emergency" twice. At the next block party you thank {grassroots} in front of the firm's banner, and the waiver waits on file for the auditors.

choices.text: Propose a fourth option: patch it, and tender.
choices.outcome: The meeting agrees, with relief, to the option you have just invented. The term contractor keeps the lift running, mostly. The tender closes on time, and so, eventually, does the lift door.

variants.body: At 8am you are on the fourteenth floor of Blk 77, because the lift is not. A resident in a wheelchair has missed two dialysis sessions. A proper tender for a new lift takes five months. {grassroots}, the {grassroots.title}, hands you a phone: a contractor who can start on Monday, if your Town Council waives the tender and answers for it later.

choices.text: Hand the phone back. The tender stays.
choices.outcome: The Town Council helps her down the stairs, with a day's notice, for every session of the tender's five months. At the new lift's opening she tells you there are 168 steps.

choices.text: Take the call. Monday it is.
choices.outcome: The contractor starts on Monday. The lift works by Christmas and she makes every session. The paperwork follows in January, written to fit what happened. Auditors prefer it the other way round.

choices.text: Get the term contractor out today, and tender the rest.
choices.outcome: The term contractor has the lift moving by evening, and patches it twice more by Christmas. The tender runs its five months. She does not miss a session, and never lets you forget the morning.

title: The National Bonus
body: As an office holder you are paid a National Bonus: three months' salary when the country hits four targets, up to six when it beats them, none when it misses. The four are unemployment, median income growth, income growth at the 20th percentile, and GDP growth (target: 2 to 4 per cent). The formula is public. Your new portfolio moves two of the four.

choices.text: Push the policy that lifts incomes at the 20th percentile.
choices.outcome: It is expensive, unglamorous and slow, and it works. It also lifts one of the four indicators in your own bonus formula. Both things are true, and nobody, ever, mentions the second one.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.
choices.outcome: Cleaner and faster, and it moves the one figure everyone watches. Your National Bonus comes in at six months, the maximum. You do not look closely at the annex on who gained.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether we should be paid on indicators we set.
choices.outcome: The question is received with great seriousness and complete stillness, and minuted. It is answered thoroughly and not at all. You are now a particular kind of colleague, and the minute stays on file.

variants.body: The Public Service Division sends you a three-page note on your pay as an office holder. Page two explains the National Bonus: three months' salary if four national targets for jobs, incomes and growth are met, up to six if they are beaten, none if missed. Page three lists the indicators your ministry can move. Two of them are in your in-tray.

choices.text: Push the policy for incomes at the 20th percentile.
choices.outcome: It is slow, costly and unglamorous, and it works. It also moves one of the four indicators on page two. Nobody, at any point, mentions page two.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.
choices.outcome: Quicker and cleaner, and it moves the figure everyone watches. Your bonus comes in at six months, the maximum. The annex on who gained is on page nine, and you stop reading at page eight.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether we should be paid on indicators we move.
choices.outcome: The question is heard in complete stillness, and minuted. It is answered at length without being answered at all. Colleagues now choose their words near you, and the minute is filed where it can be found.

variants.body: Your ministry's chief economist explains the National Bonus on a whiteboard: three months' salary for office holders when four national targets for jobs, incomes and growth are hit, up to six when they are beaten. She is brisk until she reaches the line saying who it is paid to. Then she slows down. Two of the four move with policies already on your desk.

choices.text: Choose the policy that lifts the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: It is expensive and slow, and in two years it works. It also lifts one of the lines on the whiteboard. The economist wipes the whiteboard clean before anyone can photograph it.

choices.text: Choose the policy that lifts headline GDP.
choices.outcome: The headline figure moves first and fastest. Your National Bonus comes in at six months, the most the formula allows. The economist's slide on who gained is moved to the appendix.

choices.text: Ask the other ministers whether this is how ministers should be paid.
choices.outcome: Your colleagues hear the question in silence and minute it with care. It is answered fully, and not at all. People adjust how they speak near you, and the minute stays in the file.

title: The Correction Direction
body: A post about your ministry's scheme is going viral. It is wrong in two places and, awkwardly, right in the third. Under POFMA you can have a correction notice attached to it, fixing the two wrong points in public and saying nothing about the third. Or you can answer the post yourself, and admit the point it got right.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: The correction notice appears. It is factually unimpeachable and fixes two of the three points. The third keeps circulating, now with a grievance attached: the government corrected everything except the part that was true.

choices.text: Answer the third point publicly instead.
choices.outcome: At 11pm you concede the point in a Facebook post, in your own words. It is shared more than anything your ministry has ever published, half the time by people who dislike you. You are now on record as having admitted it.

variants.body: A HardwareZone thread about your ministry's scheme has reached its fortieth page. The first post, which everyone quotes, is wrong about the eligibility age, wrong about the payout, and right about the waiting time. A POFMA correction direction would fix the two errors in public and leave the waiting time standing. You could also reply yourself.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: A correction notice is pinned above the first post, fixing the age and the payout. Page forty-one is about the waiting time. Nobody corrected that, because it was right, and the thread has noticed.

choices.text: Reply in the thread, and concede the waiting time.
choices.outcome: You reply under your own name: two corrections and one concession. The thread is polite for nearly a page, then returns to the waiting time, now quoting you as the office holder who admitted it.

variants.body: A retired officer from your ministry has posted a long critique of its scheme, with three diagrams. Two are wrong. The third is right, to the decimal: he has redrawn, from memory, a chart from an internal paper he once worked on. A POFMA correction direction would fix the two wrong diagrams and leave the right one up.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: The correction notice runs above the post and fixes two diagrams. The third stays up, uncorrected, and becomes the most widely shared chart your ministry has ever produced.

choices.text: Redraw the third diagram yourself, in public.
choices.outcome: You post the third diagram again, with the real numbers and a sentence admitting the problem. The retired officer shares it with one word, "Better." Your officials do not share it.

title: The Reshuffle
body: A Cabinet reshuffle is coming: the Prime Minister will move ministers between ministries, and has asked to see you on Thursday to hear where you would like to go. Taking on a hard ministry and surviving it is how ministers reach the top jobs. Staying put is comfortable, and rarely leads further. {mp} has already told you it is good news. {mp} does not know either.

choices.text: Ask for the hard ministry nobody wants.
choices.outcome: Housing, health or transport: something with a queue, a waiting list and a headline every week. You are given it at once, and the speed tells you it was going to be yours anyway. Survive it, and the top jobs open up.

choices.text: Ask to stay where you are.
choices.outcome: You stay. It is pleasant and important, and nobody, including you, will ever find out whether you could have handled something harder.

variants.body: A Cabinet reshuffle, moving ministers between ministries, will be announced on Monday. On Friday the Prime Minister's principal private secretary calls to ask whether you have "any preference you would like noted". A hard ministry is where ministers are tested for the top jobs; staying is safe. The call lasts ninety seconds. {mp} has already heard about it.

choices.text: Note a preference for the hardest ministry going.
choices.outcome: You name housing, health and transport. On Monday you are given one of them, announced so smoothly that the press release was plainly typed before the call. Survive it, and you will be in line for more.

choices.text: Note a preference for staying put.
choices.outcome: Your preference is noted in ninety seconds and honoured on Monday. You stay, in a ministry that runs well, as it did before you and will after you.

variants.body: A Cabinet reshuffle is due, and a newspaper's graphic puts your face in three different ministries, each with a question mark. {mp} sends you all three, with emojis. The Prime Minister's office wants twenty minutes on Thursday to hear where you would like to go. Hard ministries are how ministers rise. Staying is safe.

choices.text: Ask for whichever ministry has the longest queue.
choices.outcome: Inside the twenty minutes you are given housing, health or transport, whichever has the worst week coming. The newspaper says, for a week, that its graphic had guessed it.

choices.text: Ask to stay where you are.
choices.outcome: You stay, which the graphic had not considered. Your diary for the next five years looks very like your diary for the last five.

title: The Succession
body: The Prime Minister is stepping down, and the next generation of ministers must agree on a successor. The process is informal, which means it is decided entirely by people in a room. You are in the room, and so is the other front-runner. Put yourself forward and you may become Prime Minister. Back the other, and you get a senior portfolio but never the top job.

choices.text: Put yourself forward.
choices.outcome: You say it plainly, against convention. The room absorbs it. Nothing is decided that day, but your name is now one of the two being weighed, instead of one of the nine being listed.

choices.text: Back the other candidate. Ask for a senior portfolio.
choices.outcome: The other candidate wins, as everyone expected once you had spoken, and knows exactly who delivered it. You get everything you asked for. You will spend the rest of your career as the most powerful minister who is not Prime Minister.

title: The Work
body: A scheme goes out on time because you, {peer} and three other people made it. It will never have your name on it. Nobody's name is on it; that is how you know it is real.

choices.text: Do the work well.
choices.outcome: It goes out on time. Nobody mentions it, which is what "on time" earns you.

choices.text: Do the work, and be seen doing it.
choices.outcome: You present it at the divisional meeting with four slides more than it needed. Two people now know your name who did not. {peer}, who made half the slides, is not mentioned.

choices.text: Coast. You have earned a quiet year.
choices.outcome: You leave at six every day for a year, eat dinner at a normal hour, and it costs you exactly what you thought it would.

You clear forty-one papers and write one sentence you are proud of, which nobody notices.
A minute you wrote is quoted back to you months later as the ministry's position, and you correct nobody.
The system you fixed in March stops generating complaints, and nobody connects the two.
A paper you wrote goes upwards under someone else's covering note, which is the paper's best outcome.
You catch an error in a figure three divisions had cleared, and correct it without a reply-all.
A process you redesigned is copied by another ministry, without the footnote crediting yours.
1: You present the scheme at three forums, and by the third you are the scheme.
Your name is on the slide, the email and the photograph, for work that was mostly last year's.
Someone from another ministry greets you by name in the lift: you have been seen, and the lift is evidence.
You present the scheme at a lunchtime talk, with your photograph on the poster and the team in the footnotes.
Your scheme gets a feature on the intranet, with a photograph of you pointing at a chart.
You sit on four panels this year, three of them about the same scheme.
Your scheme is cited in a speech you did not write, and you are named in it, which you did arrange.
2: You do what is asked, on time and not a minute more, and nobody can find anything to complain about.
A quiet year at your desk, in which the best thing you write is your out-of-office message.
The papers come in and go out, and somewhere on your floor someone is working late, and it is not you.
Your inbox reaches zero twice this year, which on your floor is treated as a rumour.
You attend every meeting on time and speak at none of them, and nobody minutes the difference.
Your to-do list is shorter in December than it was in January, mostly by deletion.
A year of steady output, measured mostly in the emails you did not send.

variants.body: A form that citizens fill in has eleven fields. Seven of them ask for things the government already knows. Removing them takes four agencies, two legal opinions and a year of meetings that will never be minuted as important.

choices.text: Do the work properly.
choices.outcome: Three fields go. The other four turn out to be required by a regulation nobody can find the reason for. Three is a good year.

choices.text: Do the work, and make sure the right people see it.
choices.outcome: Your one-page note on the three fields is circulated as "a good example of citizen-centric design". You will be asked to give the talk.

choices.text: Let the agencies sort it out among themselves.
choices.outcome: They do not. The form keeps its eleven fields. You keep your evenings, which you decide were also a public good.

variants.body: This year's work is a review of a review: what was recommended three years ago, what was done, and why the difference is described as "phased implementation".

choices.text: Write it straight.
choices.outcome: Your review says what happened. It is accepted with thanks, and its recommendations are, in due course, phased.

choices.text: Write it straight, and present it yourself.
choices.outcome: You show the gap between recommendation and implementation in a chart so clear that two directors ask for the slide. One of them later uses it against you, admiringly.

choices.text: Write it the way the last one was written.
choices.outcome: It reads beautifully and says nothing anyone could disagree with. It takes a week. You spend the rest of the year on other things, mostly lunch.

variants.body: A hotline takes two thousand calls a week. Four hundred are the same question, which the website answers on page six. Someone has to decide whether the problem is the callers or page six.

choices.text: Fix page six.
choices.outcome: Page six becomes page one, in plain words. Calls drop by a third. The hotline team sends a cake with no message, which is the highest honour a hotline can give.

choices.text: Fix page six, and present the call figures.
choices.outcome: Your before-and-after chart travels further than the website did. Two other agencies cite it in their own papers, with your name in the footnote.

choices.text: Note it for whoever owns the website, and go home on time.
choices.outcome: Your note is clear and lands in the right inbox, where it stays. The calls continue. You are home by half past six, most days.

variants.body: A circular has to reach forty agencies by the first of the month. It is on its ninth draft, and the ninth is the first one anyone outside this building could understand.

choices.text: Send the ninth draft, on time.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the twenty-eighth. Three agencies reply that it is the clearest circular they have had this year, which in agency terms is a standing ovation.

choices.text: Send it, and brief the agencies yourself.
choices.outcome: Forty agencies, four briefings, one set of slides. By the last one you can do it without the slides, and two directors now ask for you by name.

choices.text: Leave the last draft to the next person in the chain.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the third of the month. Nobody asks why it was late, and you were home for dinner on all three days.

title: The Appraisal Conversation
body: Forty minutes, a form with six competency domains, and a reporting officer who says "I'd like you to be more visible" without specifying to whom.

choices.text: Ask directly what your ceiling is.
choices.outcome: "That's not really something we discuss." The sentence is delivered kindly and it is a complete answer.

choices.text: Agree to be more visible.
choices.outcome: You volunteer for two committees. It works, in the sense that more people have now seen you.

choices.text: Ask what she needs that isn't being done.
choices.outcome: She thinks for a moment and then tells you something real. You do it. That conversation is worth the other thirty-nine minutes.

0: Your ceiling, you are told again, is "not a helpful way to think about it", the most precise answer yet.
Forty minutes, six competency domains, and one question from you that nobody writes down.
You ask about your ceiling once more, and are offered a coaching session on curiosity.
Your question about the ceiling is recorded under "Officer's Aspirations", which is a box on the form.
You ask about your ceiling at the end of the forty minutes, when there are two left.
1: You agree to be more visible, your reporting officer agrees that you have been, and visibility is mentioned twice.
Six competency domains, one new acronym and the phrase "stretch assignment", with you nodding at the right moments.
You are more visible this year, mostly in the background of other people's photographs.
Your increased visibility is noted at a meeting you attended chiefly in order to be seen there.
Your visibility is discussed for forty minutes, in a room with no windows.
2: You ask what is not being done, and by March it is done and you are on a new list.
You ask what would have loosened this year's "very tight" ranking exercise, and, unusually, are told.
The things nobody was doing become your things, each with a thank-you for having asked.
The list of work nobody is doing gets shorter by March and longer by June, with your name at the top.
You ask what she needs, and she needs a lot, and now it is on your list instead of hers.

variants.body: It's appraisal week. HR has redesigned the form: four areas instead of six, a new section called "Aspirations", and a box for your reporting officer's overall impression that's bigger than all the others put together. Everyone knows the big box is what decides your grade.

choices.text: Ask what your overall impression says.
choices.outcome: "It's still being calibrated." Your reporting officer turns the form face down, gently. You'll find out with everyone else, when the grades come out.

choices.text: Fill in "Aspirations" with something ambitious.
choices.outcome: You write "to lead a cross-agency effort". A month later you're put on one, as an ordinary member. Your reporting officer calls it a good first step.

choices.text: Ask which of the four areas actually counts.
choices.outcome: After a pause, an honest answer: "Ownership." So you spend the year taking charge of things nobody else wanted. It shows, and it's noticed.

variants.body: Your appraisal is done over a video call, because your reporting officer is overseas. Her camera is off. Her connection is excellent. The forty minutes feel like ninety.

choices.text: Ask, plainly, where you stand.
choices.outcome: "You're doing fine." There is a long silence on the line, and then: "Fine is good." It is clearly not the whole sentence.

choices.text: Turn your camera on, and keep it on.
choices.outcome: Hers comes on too, eventually. The second half of the conversation is noticeably warmer. You are now, in a small way, visible.

choices.text: Ask what she would want done while she is away.
choices.outcome: She lists three things. You do two of them before she lands. She mentions it at the ranking meeting, which is the only meeting that matters.

variants.body: The appraisal is in a meeting room booked for thirty minutes. Your reporting officer arrives twelve minutes late, from another appraisal, carrying its form by mistake.

choices.text: Ask, while there is time, where your ceiling is.
choices.outcome: She looks at the form in her hand, which is not yours, and says that is above her pay grade. It may be the only literal thing said to you all year.

choices.text: Use the eighteen minutes to list what you did.
choices.outcome: You get through the list in eleven minutes. She writes down four items, and they are the four that end up in your ranking. You learn which four to lead with.

choices.text: Ask what she needs from you this year.
choices.outcome: She answers before she has sat down: a paper nobody has started. You start it that afternoon, and your next appraisal begins on time.

variants.body: This year's appraisal includes 360-degree feedback. One anonymous comment says you "never say no to anything from upstairs". It is meant, you think, as a complaint.

choices.text: Ask what the comment means for your ceiling.
choices.outcome: She says it is "a development point, not a ceiling point", and then that ceilings are not discussed. Both halves are true, and only one of them was an answer.

choices.text: Say you will be more visible, sideways as well as up.
choices.outcome: You start a monthly lunch for the people around you. Attendance is excellent. Next year's comment is about the lunches, and it is fond.

choices.text: Ask what she needs you to say no to.
choices.outcome: She names two things, immediately. You drop them both, and everyone around you notices before she does.

title: 11:40pm, Level 9
body: The clearance has come back with comments for the fourth time. {junior} is still at {junior.their} desk, waiting to see what you decide. The dinner you promised to be home for was at eight.

choices.text: Finish it tonight.
choices.outcome: Cleared at 1:20am, with {junior} proofreading the annexes. You are both thanked in one email of one word. Dinner is in the fridge, with a note that is mostly punctuation.

choices.text: Go. Send it in the morning.
choices.outcome: You send {junior} home first, and make it home yourself for dessert. It goes in at 8:40am and the world does not end, and you note carefully that the world did not end.

0: Level 9 at 11pm becomes a habit, then a reputation.
The cleaner on your floor now says goodnight to you by name.
You miss a birthday dinner and make a deadline, and both are forgotten by March, by different people.
The night guard knows your car, your floor and your usual time, which is late.
The lights on Level 9 go off on a timer at midnight, and you have learnt to wave at the sensor.
A deadline met at 1am is acknowledged at 9am with "Thanks, noted", which is all a deadline ever gets.
Your laptop battery dies at 11:58pm, mid-sentence, which you take as advice and ignore.
1: You leave at seven and send things in the morning, and the building does not fall down.
A birthday dinner, attended, while the comments on the fourth draft wait until morning, as comments always could.
You have stopped apologising for leaving on time, and two people on your floor have started doing the same.
You leave at six, the work is done by nine the next morning, and nobody can tell it from midnight.
You leave on time, the clearance comes back with comments anyway, and they are the same comments.
Dinner at eight, as promised, and the fourth draft is no worse for a night in the outbox.
You go home at seven again, and the midnight reply-all arrives without needing you in it.

variants.title: Sunday, 4pm
variants.body: Your niece's birthday party. An email from upstairs wants a brief by eight tomorrow morning, and everyone else at the table is holding cake.

choices.text: Find a quiet corner and write it now.
choices.outcome: You write it on your phone behind the cake table. It is cleared by nine. In the party photographs you are the back of a head, bent over a screen.

choices.text: Stay at the party. Write it at six tomorrow.
choices.outcome: You sing, badly, and cut the cake. The brief goes in at 7:55am. Upstairs never asks when it was written, which teaches you something you try to remember.

variants.title: 10:50pm, One Comment
variants.body: Your paper comes back with a single comment, sent at 10:50pm: "Can we tighten?" The paper is already two pages.

choices.text: Tighten it tonight.
choices.outcome: Two pages become one and a half. The half you cut was the only part anyone would have disagreed with, so the paper sails through.

choices.text: Reply that it is tight, and go to bed.
choices.outcome: You reply at 10:52pm that it is already tight, and go to bed. In the morning there is a thumbs-up, which in this building is a concession.

title: The Budget Round
body: Your bid is for eleven officers and a system. The envelope, you have been told, is flat. Every other division has been told the same, and every other bid is also for eleven of something.

choices.text: Bid big and justify every line.
choices.outcome: You get four officers and half a system, which is what you expected, having bid for eleven precisely so that four would look like a compromise.

choices.text: Bid exactly what you need.
choices.outcome: You get seventy percent of exactly what you needed, because the process assumes padding and punishes its absence.

choices.text: Don't bid. Absorb it.
choices.outcome: Everyone upstream of your bid is delighted. Your officers do the work of eleven people for three years and two of them leave.

0: You bid for eleven and get four, which is what you bid eleven for.
Budget season: every line justified, footnoted and cut by a third, as planned.
You bid big again, defend every line, and are cut back to the number you had in mind all along.
You bid for eleven officers and a system, and are given the system, which needs eleven officers.
1: You bid for exactly what you need and get two-thirds of it, which is described to you as a good outcome.
The envelope is flat and your bid is honest, and when the two meet in a spreadsheet, the spreadsheet wins.
An honest bid, funded at two-thirds again, with thanks for the realism of your projections.
Your exact bid is cut by a third, because every bid is cut by a third, and yours was exact.
2: You absorb it again, and a note of thanks arrives, the only increase you get.
Budget season, and you learn a new way to say "absorb".
No bid again; your people absorb it with you, and one of them updates a LinkedIn profile.
You absorb the cut so quietly that next year's envelope is smaller, as a vote of confidence.

variants.title: One Per Cent
variants.body: MOF has taken one per cent off every ministry's budget, its own included, to be bid back for new and emerging priorities. Your bid for eleven officers and a system has been, since Tuesday, new and emerging.

choices.text: Bid for all eleven, with a page per officer.
choices.outcome: Eleven pages, one per officer, each describing the work that officer would do. You get four back, and a note praising the pages from the people who cut them.

choices.text: Bid for exactly the gap, and say so.
choices.outcome: You bid for the gap and not a dollar more. Everyone else padded, the pool is oversubscribed, and you are funded at sixty per cent of an honest number.
