choices.text: Let the one per cent go.
choices.outcome: You absorb it. The one per cent funds someone else's new and emerging priority. Two years later that priority is merged into your division, without its officers.

variants.title: Five Minutes
variants.body: The Permanent Secretary's budget meeting: every division's bid on one screen, and a total twice the size of the ministry's envelope. Each division gets five minutes. Yours, for eleven officers and a system, is ninth.

choices.text: Bid big, and use every one of the five minutes.
choices.outcome: Five minutes, eleven officers, every line defended. The Permanent Secretary trims you to four on the spot, before anyone further up can do worse, and calls it protecting you.

choices.text: Bid exactly what you need, in two minutes.
choices.outcome: You finish in two minutes. The room is so surprised that the next division overruns by six. You are funded at two-thirds, the same as everyone who padded.

choices.text: Withdraw the bid, and give back the five minutes.
choices.outcome: The meeting ends five minutes early, and the Permanent Secretary thanks you for it by name. Your people carry the extra work for two cycles, and lose one of their number to it.

variants.title: Tab 9
variants.body: The budget template has fourteen tabs this year. Tab 9 is called Savings Identified, and the workbook will not submit while it is blank. Your bid is for eleven officers and a system. Your savings, so far, are nil.

choices.text: Fill tab 9 with savings you can defend, then bid big.
choices.outcome: Tab 9 finds savings in printing, travel and a hotline nobody calls. Tabs 10 to 14 spend them twice over. The bid is trimmed back to four officers, as everyone expected.

choices.text: Bid what you need, and leave tab 9 honest.
choices.outcome: Tab 9 says nil, with a note. The workbook will not submit a nil, so IT enters a zero for you, and the note is lost. The bid is funded at two-thirds.

choices.text: Close the workbook. Absorb it.
choices.outcome: No bid, no tab 9. The year-end summary lists your division under "units not requiring additional resources", in a slightly larger font than the others.

title: Tuesday Night
body: It is Tuesday, the night of your weekly Meet-the-People Session, where residents bring you their problems and volunteers write appeal letters for them. Tonight there are forty-one residents, a queue to the lift lobby, and a man who has come every week for two years about a case that cannot be reopened. Parliament sits tomorrow, and your speech is half written.

choices.text: See every last one of them.
choices.outcome: You finish at 12:40am and fix the two things that could be fixed. The man will be back next Tuesday, as he will be for nine more years. You finish the speech in the car, and it sounds it.

choices.text: Take the hardest cases, and write them yourself.
choices.outcome: You write eleven letters, each argued rather than copied from a template, and three succeed that would not have. Thirty residents are seen by your volunteers, who are very good, and are not you.

choices.text: Leave at ten. Finish the speech.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten, and the speech goes well in the House. The volunteers stay until one. By Thursday a resident has posted about the evening, and the post is about ten o'clock.

0: You see every resident on Tuesday nights, and the man whose case cannot be reopened now brings you kueh.
Your Meet-the-People Session runs past midnight again, and the volunteers have started bringing cushions.
The coffee shop downstairs now closes before your Meet-the-People Session does, every week.
Another Tuesday ends after midnight, with the last resident apologising for the hour and seen anyway.
A resident brings a folder of letters from three MPs before you, and you read every one.
The last resident of the night only wants to say thank you, and you stay for all forty minutes of it.
1: You write the hardest appeals yourself, and three a month now succeed that would not have.
An appeal you argued yourself is approved, and the resident thanks the volunteer who typed it, fairly.
You write the hard appeals yourself again, and one agency has started to recognise your paragraphs.
A letter you drafted on a Tuesday gets a reply by Friday, and the volunteers call it a record.
Your letters to agencies now open with the right section number, and the agencies have noticed.
A volunteer asks how you write the hard appeals, and you teach the paragraph, not the template.
2: You leave the Tuesday session at ten again, and the volunteers see the rest of the queue, very well and very tired.
A resident thanks you for something the Town Council did, and you accept on its behalf and leave at ten.
Your speech is finished by Wednesday, and the volunteers finish the queue without you, a little after midnight.
You leave Meet-the-People at ten again, and the volunteers no longer look up when the lift doors close.
Your speech is the best-prepared in the House, and the Tuesday queue is a little longer for it.
The volunteers keep a list of the residents who asked for you after ten, and give it to you monthly.

variants.title: Meet-the-People, After the Rain
variants.body: Your weekly Meet-the-People Session: a downpour at seven, so everyone comes at nine. In the queue are a family whose flat appeal has been turned down twice, and a man who wants the void deck named after his father. Parliament sits at noon tomorrow, and you have not read your papers.

choices.text: Stay until the last one is seen.
choices.outcome: Past one in the morning. The void deck will not be renamed, and you tell him so, kindly enough that he shakes your hand twice. You read your papers for the sitting in the car.

choices.text: Take the family's appeal, and write it yourself.
choices.outcome: Two pages, citing the right paragraph. The appeal succeeds on the third try, which the family credits to persistence and you credit to the paragraph. A volunteer sees the void deck man.

choices.text: Leave the volunteers to finish. Read your papers.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten and are word-perfect in the House. The volunteers stay until one. The following Tuesday, the void deck man asks, pointedly, whether you are staying tonight.

variants.title: Tuesday Night, the Lift
variants.body: Thirty residents at tonight's Meet-the-People Session, all about one thing: a lift that has been under upgrading for eleven months. Nobody is angry with you. Everybody would like you to be angry on their behalf, tonight, in person. Parliament sits tomorrow, and you have papers to read.

choices.text: See every one of them, one by one.
choices.outcome: Thirty conversations about the same lift, until one in the morning. They go home feeling heard. That is not a lift, but it is not nothing.

choices.text: Write about the lift properly, tonight.
choices.outcome: Your letter names the contractor, the start date and the eleven months. A new completion date arrives within the week, and is met. Volunteers saw the residents, and the residents noticed.

choices.text: Let the volunteers take the rest.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten to prepare for the House. Twenty-nine residents are seen about the lift. The thirtieth wanted you, and mentions it at every block party for a year.

title: The Walkabout
body: It is 7:20am at the wet market in your ward, on a walkabout with a camera crew. A stallholder has strong and specific views about the price of chillies, and is delighted to share them, at volume. Fourteen stalls are still to go, and every one of them votes.

choices.text: Listen to her properly, on camera.
choices.outcome: Four minutes of her talking and you not interrupting. The clip is shared widely, and the comments are, unusually, kind. The last fourteen stalls get nine seconds each.

choices.text: Keep moving. Every stall gets a handshake.
choices.outcome: Every stall in forty minutes. The photographs are excellent, and nobody remembers a word you said.

choices.text: Take her number. Call her tonight, off camera.
choices.outcome: You call at nine. She talks for forty minutes about chillies, supply chains and her nephew. None of it is filmed, and two of her points end up in your letter to the ministry.

0: Wet markets at 7am, with cameras, until you know the price of chillies better than the price of anything else.
On a walkabout an auntie says you looked thinner on television, and you hear out the rest of it, about the lift.
A stallholder you once listened to on camera now greets you with the price of something new.
Another walkabout, another auntie, and four minutes of footage about her lift that the news runs in full.
A fishmonger explains the price of fish to you on camera, and the clip is shared mostly by fishmongers.
You hear out a complaint about a bus route on camera, and the route is changed, though not because of the camera.
1: A walkabout in the rain, on schedule, and the photograph of you under someone else's umbrella does very well.
Eleven market stalls in forty minutes: everyone gets a handshake and nobody gets a sentence.
Fourteen stalls, fourteen handshakes and a volunteer one step behind you with hand sanitiser.
The walkabout keeps to time, and the photographs are better than anything anyone said.
Every stall gets a handshake before nine, and you are in the car by a quarter past, as planned.
The walkabout is so punctual that the stallholders now time their breaks by it.
2: You take numbers at walkabouts and call them at night, and your call log becomes the best map of the ward.
Three phone numbers on a napkin from the wet market, and you call all three that evening, off camera.
You call a stallholder back about her rent, and she tells the next stall, and the next.
A resident you called one night tells the whole RC, and that is now what the RC knows you for.
Your evening calls now take longer than the walkabouts, and settle more.
A hawker you called back about her lease tells you the next week that it was renewed, as if you did it.

variants.title: The Hawker Centre
variants.body: A lunchtime walkabout at a hawker centre in your ward, with photographers. The uncle at the drinks stall wants to explain, in detail, why his rent has gone up and what should be done about it. The other stalls are watching to see how long you give him.

choices.text: Sit down and hear him out.
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes, one kopi going cold, and a written follow-up on his rent. The one photographer who stayed gets the best picture of the day. The next three stalls get none.

choices.text: Buy a kopi, smile, and keep moving.
choices.outcome: You pay for the kopi, smile for the photograph and move on. In the photograph, he is still talking.

choices.text: Ask for his number. Call him tonight.
choices.outcome: You call after dinner. He has prepared notes. His rent case goes to the agency under your name the next morning, and there is no photograph of any of it.

variants.title: The Estate Visit
variants.body: An estate walkabout in your ward: eight blocks before lunch, then a ribbon to cut, with cameras all the way. A resident on a mobility scooter wants to show you a ramp that does not quite reach the kerb. It is two blocks off your route, and the ribbon is on a schedule.

choices.text: Go and look at the ramp.
choices.outcome: You walk the ramp with her, slowly, cameras behind you. It is two centimetres short, and fixed within a fortnight. The ribbon is cut forty minutes late, to applause from people who wanted lunch.

choices.text: Promise someone will look, and stay on schedule.
choices.outcome: Someone does look, eventually. The ribbon is cut on time, by you, in a photograph that is very well lit.

choices.text: Get her number. Send someone this afternoon.
choices.outcome: An officer measures the ramp at four: two centimetres short. It is fixed within a fortnight. She sends you a photograph of herself using it, and nobody else ever sees it.

title: The Parliamentary Question
body: A Member has filed a Parliamentary Question about a scheme your ministry runs, and you must answer it in the House. The question is good and sharply drafted, and the honest answer is not flattering. The brief your officials wrote is accurate, and answers a slightly different question. Whatever you say goes into Hansard for good.

choices.text: Answer it straight, and say what you will do.
choices.outcome: You concede the point and say what you are doing about it. The follow-up question is gentler than it would have been, because there is nothing left to prise open. Your answer goes into Hansard, word for word.

choices.text: Read the brief, which answers a nearby question.
choices.outcome: Technically responsive, substantively elsewhere. It takes skill and you have it, and the clip will stay online for longer than the scheme.

choices.text: Promise a full written answer, and write it properly.
choices.outcome: The written answer runs to four pages, with tables, and is the most complete account the ministry has ever given of the scheme. The Member reads it. So does one researcher.

0: At Question Time you answer the question that was actually asked, and people still notice.
Seven questions this sitting, and two of your answers make the news for being short and true.
A Member files a question expecting a brief, gets an answer instead, and files another.
Your straight answers are now quoted back to you in supplementaries, so somebody read them.
You give the House the actual number, and the Member who asked has no supplementary ready.
Your answer in the House is one paragraph shorter than the brief: you cut the paragraph that dodged.
1: At Question Time you answer a question that was nearly the one asked.
A sharp supplementary meets a smooth reply; Hansard records both, and the papers record the reply.
Question Time again, and the brief answers a question your officials found easier.
Your replies this sitting are smooth enough that the supplementaries slide straight off them.
The brief is read in full, accurately, and a Member asks the original question again in other words.
At Question Time you read the brief so well that nobody can quite say which question it answered.
2: Seven questions this sitting, and the full written answers follow, as promised, with tables.
Another four-page written answer, and a university researcher cites three of them in a paper, with footnotes.
Another written answer to a Parliamentary Question goes out, longer than the question and shorter than its annex.
Your written answers come with tables, and one Member starts filing questions just to get them.
Your written answer is footnoted so thoroughly that the Member who asked thanks you for the reading list.
Another question becomes another written answer, delivered on the date you promised, and that is the news.

variants.title: Question Time
variants.body: At Question Time a Member asks whether your ministry will review a rule that residents complain about at every Meet-the-People Session. It is already under review, but nothing is decided, and the ministry is saving the news for an announcement in March, with a backdrop. What you say now goes into Hansard.

choices.text: Say it is under review, and what is being looked at.
choices.outcome: You say so, plainly, and name the three things being looked at. The Member thanks you. The announcement in March makes smaller news than it would have, backdrop and all.

choices.text: Say the ministry keeps all its rules under review.
choices.outcome: This is true of every rule and says nothing about this one. The Member points that out. Hansard records you both, and the announcement in March gets the headline.

choices.text: Offer the Member a full written reply once it is decided.
choices.outcome: The written reply goes out the week after the decision: three pages, complete. The Member reads all of it, and files a new question about the parts the announcement left out.

variants.title: The Supplementary
variants.body: You have answered a Parliamentary Question about your ministry, and it went well. Then the Member rises with a follow-up question, the one your officials said would not come, and your brief has nothing on it. The House is waiting, and Hansard is recording.

choices.text: Answer it straight, without the brief.
choices.outcome: You say you do not have the figure to hand, then say what you do know. It is enough. Your officials send a note that reads, in full, "Well handled."

choices.text: Answer a nearby question the brief does cover.
choices.outcome: The answer is fluent, confident and about something else. The Member says, "That was not my question," and is quoted the next morning in full.

choices.text: Offer to write to the Member, and do it properly.
choices.outcome: You write two pages, with the figure you did not have to hand. The Member quotes your letter in the next debate, more kindly than you had expected.

title: The Ministry Townhall
body: You are hosting your ministry's townhall: four hundred officers, and an anonymous question board on the screen behind you. One question has far more upvotes than the rest. It is about workload, and it is not polite. Every officer in the room is waiting to see whether you read it out.

choices.text: Read it out and answer it.
choices.outcome: You read it in full, rude part included, and answer it for eleven minutes without notes. The room changes temperature. Nobody repeats anything else from the townhall, inside the ministry or out.

choices.text: Address the theme without reading it.
choices.outcome: You speak warmly about wellbeing and the importance of a sustainable pace. Four hundred officers understand precisely what has happened, and so does the question board.

0: The workload question tops the townhall board again, you read it out again, and the upvotes stop being anonymous in spirit.
Four hundred officers, one microphone, and a rude question read out in full: the only part of the townhall anyone repeats.
An officer thanks you at the lift for reading the rude townhall question out, in a whisper, in case it counts.
You read the townhall's top question out in full, and the next year one officer signs her name to hers.
The townhall question about workload is read out again, and this time a director in the front row nods.
1: The townhall's top question is about workload, and you address its theme, warmly.
Your townhall slides circulate, unofficially, as an example of what a townhall can be.
The townhall runs to time and the theme is addressed, while the question waits on the board like a queue number.
At the townhall you answer the theme of the top question so warmly that HR asks to use it in a module.
The theme of the top question becomes the title of next year's townhall, and that counts as an answer.

variants.title: The Curated Questions
variants.body: At your ministry's townhall this year, the questions were submitted in advance and curated, so that nothing awkward would come up. Four hundred officers are watching. An officer at the back puts her hand up anyway, and the room turns to see whether you will take her question.

choices.text: Take her question.
choices.outcome: It is about promotions, and it is fair. You answer it partly, and say that it is only partly. Afterwards, the curated questions are the part nobody remembers.

choices.text: Say there will be time at the end.
choices.outcome: There is no time at the end. There was never going to be, and four hundred officers watched her lower her hand.

variants.title: The Survey Results
variants.body: Your ministry's staff survey is back, and you are presenting it at the townhall. Most numbers went up. One fell a long way: whether officers feel safe raising concerns. Four hundred of them will see which number you put first.

choices.text: Put that number on the first slide.
choices.outcome: The first slide is the bad number, in large type, and you talk about it for ten minutes. Two directors look at the floor. Four hundred officers look at you.

choices.text: Lead with the numbers that went up.
choices.outcome: The deck opens on engagement, up four points. The other number is on slide nineteen. Most of the room had found slide nineteen before you started.

title: A Year Without Incident
body: Everything runs. The schemes run. You go to Bintan in June and nothing breaks while you are gone, which is either a compliment or a warning.

choices.text: Use it to fix something nobody asked you to fix.
choices.outcome: You get a process fixed that has annoyed eleven thousand people for a decade. It takes a year and it is never announced.

choices.text: Use it to build your network.
choices.outcome: Coffee, lunches, and a very great deal of being remembered. It is not work. It is, unmistakably, the job.

choices.text: Use it to rest.
choices.outcome: You rest. It turns out you needed it more than the ministry needed the other two options.

0: Nothing breaks all year, which you suspect is not a coincidence and cannot prove.
You use a quiet year to fix a process that annoyed people since before you arrived, and never announce it.
You spend a quiet year fixing a form nobody asked you to fix, and three people quietly stop complaining.
A quiet year, and you clear a backlog that predates three directors, without telling any of them.
You fix the meeting-room booking system in a quiet year, and the queue for the big room quietly disappears.
In a quiet year you write down a process that existed only in one retiring officer's head.
1: A quiet year and forty lunches, thirty of which you remember, which is about average.
You attend everything you are invited to, and by December you are invited to more.
A quiet year of coffees in the same three cafés, with people who will remember you as "helpful".
A quiet year of networking, after which three people you have met once describe you as "a friend".
In a quiet year you join two committees, both for the networking and one of them for the food.
A quiet year of receptions, where you learn to hold a plate, a glass and a business card at once.
2: Bintan in June, where you check your email only twice, which is progress.
A quiet year, and somewhere someone writes "steady" about you and means it kindly.
A quiet year, and you take all your leave, which HR's system flags as unusual.
You rest, and the schemes keep running without you, which is reassuring and very slightly insulting.
A quiet year, and you leave at six without a single email asking where you are.
A quiet year, and you read three books, none of them about leadership.

variants.body: No crisis, no reorganisation, no parliamentary question with your name in it. Your diary has white space for the first time in years, and everyone around you has noticed, and is pretending not to.

choices.text: Use it to fix something small and permanent.
choices.outcome: You fix the thing that has made every new joiner's first week worse for a decade. Nobody thanks you. The new joiners never find out what it used to be like.

choices.text: Use it for the lunches you keep postponing.
choices.outcome: Eleven lunches, four dinners and one kopi at a hawker centre that turns out to matter more than the dinners. People remember you now in a way they did not.

choices.text: Use it to sleep.
choices.outcome: You sleep. Your doctor, who has been saying things for three years, says nothing, which is the nicest thing a doctor has ever said to you.

variants.body: Nothing much happens to you this year. The most discussed thing on your floor is the new coffee machine, which has nine settings; everyone uses the same one. A quiet year is a chance to do something for yourself.

choices.text: Read every file you've been forwarded and never opened.
choices.outcome: In the unopened files you find two problems you can fix, and one that someone should have fixed three years ago. You fix the two, and write a note about the third that nobody will enjoy receiving.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the people who decide things.
choices.outcome: You become the person who knows where everything is and who to ask. It isn't a title, but it gets you into rooms.

choices.text: Take your leave, all of it.
choices.outcome: You take every day of leave you're owed. The office copes without you, which is either reassuring or not.

title: The Counter
body: You're a Management Executive at the {ministry}, eight months in. Before this you spent four years working a public service counter, and you're still finishing a part-time degree at night. Your reporting officer, {senior}, has set up a team to redesign how the public applies for a scheme. You're the most junior person on it, and the only one who has ever worked a counter.

choices.text: Tell the team exactly why the new design will fail.
choices.outcome: You describe, from memory, the eleven things a person at a counter is actually holding in their hands. The room goes quiet, and the design changes. {senior} asks where you worked before, and listens to the whole answer.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the pilot show them.
choices.outcome: The pilot fails exactly the way you knew it would, and you're the one asked to fix it. Being listened to the first time would have been less work.

title: The Last Paper
body: Your part-time degree is down to one Saturday exam, after six years of evening classes. It's also the busiest month of the year at work. {peer}, who joined the service the same year as you, finished {peer.their} degree at twenty-two, full-time, on a scholarship. Finishing yours opens jobs a diploma doesn't.

choices.text: Sit the exam and finish it.
choices.outcome: Second Upper. Nobody at work marks it, because nobody at work knew. But it changes which jobs you can apply for, and, more slowly, which ones you think you can.

choices.text: Defer it. Work needs you this month.
choices.outcome: The busy month is followed by another, and another. You finish the degree four years later, by which time the jobs it would have opened have gone to other people.

title: Someone From Before
body: At an inter-agency meeting you recognise the chair. Years ago, before the degree, you sat two desks apart at the same statutory board, on the same grade.

choices.text: Speak to her afterwards.
choices.outcome: She remembers you immediately and without condescension, which you had not dared expect. She puts you on two committees that matter and tells you, plainly, which one to care about.

choices.text: Say nothing. She has moved on.
choices.outcome: She has not moved on; she simply did not see you. You think about the two desks for a week afterwards and then you stop.

title: The Board Takes a Second Look
body: A promotion board has been asked, unusually, to revisit an officer whose record does not match their grade. The officer is you.

choices.text: Make the case yourself, in writing.
choices.outcome: Four pages. You do not argue that you have been treated unfairly, which would have been true and useless; you argue what you would do with the next grade. The estimate is revised. Nobody tells you by how much.

choices.text: Let the record speak.
choices.outcome: The record does speak, and it is a good record, and it moves them slightly less than four pages would have.

title: The Figure, Cited
body: A review of the scheme's design cites a utilisation rate of 31%, attributed to a slide from your division. {Asker} asks, carefully, who presented it.

options.text: {senior}, who once asked you for a range,

choices.text: Say it was you.
choices.outcome: {Asker.short} nods slowly. You watch your name move from one column of something to another.

choices.text: Say it was a team effort.
choices.outcome: It was not, entirely. Your team knows that, and it does you more good with them than the other answer would have done upstairs.

title: Paragraph Four
body: The consultancy's recommendations have been implemented, and have failed in exactly the way your minute paper, two years older, predicted in paragraph four. Someone has found paragraph four.

choices.text: Let paragraph four speak for itself.
choices.outcome: It is read aloud at a meeting you are not at. Afterwards, three people forward it to you, each believing they are the first.

choices.text: Offer to fix it.
choices.outcome: They let you. It takes a year, and a consultancy is engaged to evaluate your fix.

title: The Thing Nobody Announced
body: Every ministry that announced something at COS is now explaining delays. Your Minister, who announced nothing, is the only one who is not. He has noticed.

choices.text: Bring him the pilot, now that it is ready.
choices.outcome: He announces it at the next COS, on time and as described. He mentions your division by name, which Ministers do not do.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let him draw the conclusion.
choices.outcome: He draws it. When his Permanent Secretary next asks which divisions he rates, yours is the first he names, in front of the person who writes your ranking.

title: The Raw Feedback
body: A think tank has analysed the raw feedback you published. Its paper is cited in Parliament, approvingly, by both sides. Your Permanent Secretary forwards it to you with no comment, which from her is a great deal of comment.

choices.text: Reply with one line.
choices.outcome: "Thank you. It was their feedback." She replies within a minute, which nobody has ever seen her do.

choices.text: Write the follow-up nobody asked for.
choices.outcome: It becomes the template for the next national conversation, which uses four pillars.

title: The Decision Paper
body: The Inter-Ministry Committee has been dissolved. Its replacement has adopted your decision paper as its terms of reference, and someone has left your name in the footer.

choices.text: Leave your name on it.
choices.outcome: The footer travels further than you ever have. A Deputy Secretary you have never met asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it off before it circulates.
choices.outcome: It circulates anonymously, which in this building is how people find out who wrote it.

title: The Third Point
body: A while ago you publicly admitted the one point that a viral post about your ministry's scheme got right. Now the scheme has been quietly amended to fix exactly that. {journalist}, {journalist.aTitle} at the paper, has noticed that you were the only office holder who admitted it, and asks you about it on the record.

choices.text: Take the question on the record.
choices.outcome: The piece runs on a Sunday. Its headline calls you "candid", a word your press secretary asks you never to be again.

choices.text: Credit the post's author.
choices.outcome: The post's author is astonished, then gracious, then a reliable critic of yours for the rest of your career. You decide to take that as a compliment.

title: Hansard
body: A newer Member quotes you in her own speech, word for word, with attribution. Someone on the front bench looks up the original.

choices.text: Send her a note.
choices.outcome: She frames it. You hear about this from four people, none of whom are her.

choices.text: Say nothing.
choices.outcome: The quote goes round without you. It turns out to be the most-shared thing you have ever said.

title: Terms of Reference
body: Some years ago you asked the other ministers whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set themselves. Now a committee has been appointed to review political salaries, and your question appears, unattributed, as item three of its terms of reference. The committee is inviting submissions.

choices.text: Make a submission under your own name.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for your submission. Its report adjusts the formula by one percentage point, which it describes as significant. Your name is in the annex, where colleagues will find it.

choices.text: Let item three do the work.
choices.outcome: Item three does very little work on its own. But you were seen not to make a fuss, and among colleagues that counts for something.

title: The Annual Report
body: The statutory board you were sent to fix has published its annual report. For the first time in four years it contains no restatements, and the auditors' letter is one page long.

choices.text: Ask to come back.
choices.outcome: You come back to a better office than the one you left. It turns out the secondment was a proving ground. Nobody tells you this; they simply act as if it had always been obvious.

choices.text: Ask to stay and finish it.
choices.outcome: You stay. The board becomes the case study on the leadership programme, taught by someone who was never there.

title: Polling Day, Again
body: Parliament is dissolved on a Tuesday, so there is a general election within weeks and your seat is up again. Lose it, and your political career is over. Nobody is surprised; the tents went up in the void decks a fortnight ago. This time your branch chairman has started using the word "swing" in sentences about you.

choices.text: Campaign on the record.
choices.outcome: You stand on a lorry and read out what has been delivered in the ward since the last election. Some of the numbers are yours.

choices.text: Walk every block, every night, for nine days.
choices.outcome: Nine nights, four hundred lift lobbies, and one pair of shoes you will never wear again.

lines: Another general election, and on the campaign lorry you read out the ward's numbers, some of them yours.
The thank-you lorry takes the same route as last time, down to the stop for kopi at the same coffee shop.
Nine days of campaigning, one rally, and a sample count that tells everyone the result before the real one does.
Your ward's result is among the first in, and your branch treats this as a personal achievement.
Election posters go up at the first permitted minute and come down by the date on the permit.
On Cooling-off Day nobody may campaign, so you spend it reading the comments, and wish you could.
Nomination Day, nine days of walkabouts, and a result your branch chairman predicted, in writing, to within a point.
By the end of the campaign you can rank every coffee shop in the ward by its kopi, privately.

title: The Indicators
body: Your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets, and it sets part of your pay. Office holders get a National Bonus: three months' salary when the country hits its targets for growth, jobs, median incomes and incomes at the 20th percentile, up to six when it beats them. Growth is strong. You can push one line, not all of them.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Growth comes in a little under forecast, which in a strong year is noticed, and your National Bonus drops to two months. The commentary uses the word "moderate" four times.

choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast, and your National Bonus is five months. Incomes at the 20th percentile rise too, slightly, the way a small boat rises when a larger one goes past.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses its target by a tenth of a point, and the formula pays no National Bonus at all. The chart is still a good chart.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile grow faster than the median, which has not happened in six years, and your bonus is four months. The chart goes into the Budget speech, in colour.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Change nothing that is working.
choices.outcome: Every target is met to the decimal place, which pays the standard three months. Nothing is announced, because nothing has changed, and other ministries copy the plan.

variants.body: Finance writes to every ministry: growth is strong, so the next three Budgets have room in them. Your Permanent Secretary has drafted three plans and stacked them on your desk, in an order that is a recommendation. Whichever you sign also sets your National Bonus: three months' salary for hitting the national targets on growth, jobs and incomes, up to six for beating them.

choices.text: Sign the plan that backs the investment push.
choices.outcome: Two plants and a data centre are brought forward, growth comes in above forecast, and your bonus is five months. The 20th percentile rises a little, carried along. The other plans go into a drawer.

choices.text: Sign the one for wage support at the bottom.
choices.outcome: Wage support for the lowest-paid goes into the Budget, their incomes outgrow the median by the next survey, and your bonus is four months. Finance writes, twice, to ask whether the support is temporary.

choices.text: Sign the one that changes nothing.
choices.outcome: The plan that changes nothing changes nothing, on schedule. Every target is met, so your bonus is the standard three months. Your Permanent Secretary files the other two drafts in a folder marked "Later".

variants.body: Your ministry's chief economist has one chart for the next three Budgets: growth strong, incomes at the 20th percentile flat. "You can move either line," the economist says. "Not both, at this price." Both lines feed your National Bonus, which pays three months' salary when the national targets are met and up to six when they are beaten.

choices.text: Move the growth line.
choices.outcome: The growth line climbs above forecast, and your bonus is five months. The 20th-percentile line rises a little too, out of politeness. The economist relabels the chart "broad-based".

choices.text: Move the 20th-percentile line.
choices.outcome: The lower line overtakes the median's growth and holds, and your bonus is four months. The economist prints the chart on A3, which economists do not do.

choices.text: Move neither. Hit the targets as planned.
choices.outcome: Both lines stay inside their target bands, which pays the standard three months. The economist calls it the most boring chart of the decade, and is privately proud of it.

variants.body: At a tripartite dinner, a union leader and an employers' federation president sit either side of you, each with a plan for your ministry's next three Budgets. The employers' plan pushes growth; the union's pushes the lowest wages. Either moves your National Bonus, which pays three months' salary for hitting the national targets and up to six for beating them.

choices.text: Back the employers' plan for growth.
choices.outcome: The investment push lands, growth comes in strong, and your bonus is five months. At the next dinner the union leader sits across the room, and raises a glass to you anyway.

choices.text: Back the union's plan for the lowest-paid.
choices.outcome: Wages at the bottom outgrow the median, and your bonus is four months. The federation's president sends a note of congratulations that is mostly about costs.

choices.text: Back neither. Keep the plan you have.
choices.outcome: Both send notes saying they understand. The targets are met, so your bonus is the standard three months. The two notes are filed together, which neither of them would like.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again
headline.body: Growth is strong again, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you went for the biggest headline numbers, and your officials have redrafted that plan with the dates changed in pen. Whatever you sign now becomes the ministry's standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, in good years and bad, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Sign it as it is.
choices.outcome: Signed in pen, beside the old dates. Growth comes in above forecast again, your bonus is five months, and the plan will now renew itself. Nobody asks what else it could have been.

choices.text: Cross it out. Put the 20th percentile first.
choices.outcome: Your officials redraft three years of work in a fortnight, and Finance asks in writing why a working plan has changed. Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median by spring, and this is now the standing plan.

choices.text: Cross it out. Bank the targets instead.
choices.outcome: The new plan is the old one with its ambitions removed, and Finance minutes it as a "recalibration". The targets are met exactly, for the standard three months, and from now on the plan renews itself.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again
lowest.body: Growth is strong, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you put incomes at the 20th percentile first, and that chart now hangs in the ministry lobby, framed. Your officials' draft keeps it climbing. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, in good years and bad, without being put to you again.

choices.text: Take the chart down. Push headline GDP this time.
choices.outcome: The chart comes down on a Saturday, so nobody sees it go. Growth comes in above forecast, and growth-first is now the standing plan. Your chief economist asks, in a long email, what the last three years were for.

choices.text: Sign it. Keep the chart climbing.
choices.outcome: Signed without a meeting. Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median for another cycle, your bonus is four months, and the plan will now roll on by itself. The lobby chart is replaced by a larger one.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Let the chart level off.
choices.outcome: The new plan meets its targets and moves nothing, and it is now the plan for good. The chart levels off and comes down, the lobby gets a potted plant, and Finance writes to say it liked the chart.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again
steady.body: Growth is strong, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you chose the safe plan, protecting what already worked, and it did exactly what it said; other ministries now borrow it. Your officials have drafted it again. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, in good years and bad, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Stop it. Push headline GDP while the going is good.
choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast, and growth-first is the standing plan from now on. The ministries that borrowed your old plan have to give it back, and your officials rewrite three years of documents in three weeks.

choices.text: Stop it. Put the 20th percentile first.
choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median by the next survey, and that is the standing plan from now on. The ministries that borrowed your old plan ask, in writing, whether they must change theirs.

choices.text: Let it renew.
choices.outcome: It renews, and will keep renewing. The targets are met to the decimal, for the standard three months, and the plan is cited in a training course as an example of what a plan should be. It is cited nowhere else.

headline: Growth is strong, and your ministry rolls its growth-first plan into three more Budgets without asking you, as agreed.
Your officials renew the growth-first plan on their own, exactly as you told them to.
Two more plants are brought forward under your growth-first plan, announced in a press release copied from the last one.
In a strong year your standing plan pushes headline growth again, and the quarterly slide keeps its arrow pointing up.
The growth-first plan renews itself for three more Budgets, and the only edit anyone makes is to the year.
lowest: Your plan for incomes at the 20th percentile rolls into three more Budgets, and its chart gets new numbers.
Wage support for the lowest-paid is renewed without a meeting, the surest sign that it is policy now.
Finance's yearly letter asking whether the support for the lowest-paid is temporary arrives on schedule, and gets a template reply.
Your standing plan puts the lowest incomes first again, and your economists print the chart on A3, out of habit.
Another ministry adopts your plan for the lowest incomes, and sends a thank-you note with its own logo on it.
steady: The safe plan rolls into three more Budgets, and nobody in the ministry remembers a time before it.
The plan that changes nothing is renewed, unchanged, as intended.
Growth is strong and your standing plan stays steady: the targets are tracked to the decimal and nothing is announced.
Your officials renew the steady plan, and a training course adds it to its slide titled "Good Practice".
The steady plan renews itself for three more Budgets, and its only new feature is a page number.

title: The Indicators, in a Downturn
body: Exports are down for a third quarter and "retrenchment" is back in the papers. Your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets now, and the plan sets your National Bonus: three months' salary when the country hits its targets for growth, jobs and incomes, less when it misses. In a downturn it will miss something. You choose what to protect.

choices.text: Protect jobs first.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Unemployment rises anyway, by less than it would have. The indicator does not record the difference, and the formula pays no National Bonus.

choices.outcome: Unemployment holds, growth does not, and your bonus is two months. A great many people keep jobs they will never know were on a list.

choices.text: Push growth through it.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The push does not take. Growth stays flat, the 20th percentile falls, and there is no National Bonus. Nobody calls it a gamble, because it was a plan.

choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region and your bonus is four months. The speech about resilience writes itself. The jobs come back eighteen months later, in other industries, for other people.

choices.text: Cushion the lowest incomes.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The cushion holds the 20th percentile steady. The indicator only counts growing, not holding steady, so the formula pays no National Bonus.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile hold steady through the downturn, and your bonus is one month. Rent is paid on time in a great many flats. Nobody reports on rent paid on time.

variants.body: The downturn is in its fourth quarter, and Finance wants your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets by Friday. The plan also sets your National Bonus, which pays three months' salary when the national targets for growth, jobs and incomes are met, and less in a year like this. Your Permanent Secretary has drafted three versions, and has not slept much.

choices.text: Send the wage support, for jobs.
choices.outcome: The wage support goes into the Budget, firms keep workers they had already listed, and your bonus is two months. The firms fill in the forms to say so, in triplicate, grumbling.

choices.text: Send the projects, brought forward.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward and cranes go up in the west. Growth recovers ahead of the region and your bonus is four months. Finance's letter of thanks mentions the cranes, twice.

choices.text: Send the cash for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash goes out in March and is spent within a month on rent, school shoes and hawker food, as the economists had predicted to the week. Your bonus is one month.

variants.body: At Tuesday's Meet-the-People Session, three of the first ten cases are retrenchments. On Thursday your ministry settles its plan for the next three Budgets, and the plan also sets your National Bonus: three months' salary when the national targets for growth, jobs and incomes are hit, less in a downturn. The three files are still in your bag.

choices.text: Plan for jobs.
choices.outcome: The plan keeps people in work, and your bonus is two months. By spring, retrenchment cases at your Tuesday session are down to one in twenty, and that one wanted to leave anyway.

choices.text: Plan for growth. The jobs will follow it.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region and your bonus is four months. Two of the three residents find work in the new projects by spring. The third finds it in another industry, and prefers it.

choices.text: Plan for the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes hold steady and your bonus is one month. The three residents are still looking for work at Chinese New Year, but their rent is paid, and they tell you so, at length.

variants.body: Finance's officials take you through the downturn package line by line, until they reach your ministry's line. It is blank: your plan for the next three Budgets, which also sets your National Bonus, is not yet decided. The bonus pays three months' salary when the national targets are met, less when they are missed. Three options are pencilled beside the line. Everyone waits, with pens.

choices.text: Write in the jobs scheme.
choices.outcome: The jobs scheme goes in, in ink. Unemployment holds through the downturn and your bonus is two months. Growth does not hold, and Finance's officials note this, in pencil.

choices.text: Write in the growth projects.
choices.outcome: The projects go in, in ink, growth recovers ahead of the region, and your bonus is four months. An official with a very good eraser rubs out the other two options.

choices.text: Write in the cash for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash goes in, in ink, the lowest incomes hold steady, and your bonus is one month. Finance's officials ask, twice, whether it is temporary. You say yes both times.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
steady.body: The economy has turned down and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you chose the safe plan, and your officials have drafted this one the same way: jobs first, under a cover that says "For signature", not "For decision". Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Sign it. Jobs first, again.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds through the downturn, your bonus is two months, and jobs-first is now the plan for good. The press release is last cycle's, with the year changed by hand.

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward, growth recovers ahead of the region, and growth-first is the standing plan from now on. Your officials, who had expected a signature, spend March rebuilding the plan around cranes.

choices.text: Write "For decision" on it. Cushion the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The cash for the lowest incomes goes out in spring, rent is paid on time in a great many flats, and this is now the standing plan. Finance asks, twice, why the plan changed.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
headline.body: Exports have turned down, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you went for the biggest headline numbers, and your ministry now has a growth unit, with a logo. Its draft pushes growth through the downturn. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you. The unit would like to continue existing.

choices.text: Overrule the unit. Protect jobs first.
choices.outcome: Unemployment holds and growth does not, and jobs-first is now the standing plan. The growth unit is renamed the Resilience Unit, in a memo that takes eleven drafts, and nobody in it is retrenched.

choices.text: Sign it. The unit knows what it is doing.
choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region again, your bonus is four months, and the plan will now renew itself. The unit's logo goes on the Budget slide, and the papers run a shorter story than last time.

choices.text: Turn the unit to the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: The growth unit spends the downturn delivering cash to the lowest incomes, efficiently and with visible reluctance. Rent is paid on time in a great many flats, and this is the standing plan now.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again, in a Downturn
lowest.body: The downturn is official, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you put the lowest incomes first, and the payment system built for it is still running, idle, at some expense. Your officials' draft switches it back on. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Repurpose it for wage support, to keep people in work.
choices.outcome: The system is repurposed for wage support, which takes four months and a new acronym. Unemployment holds, jobs-first is now the standing plan, and the vendor bills for the acronym.

choices.text: Switch it off. Push growth through.
choices.outcome: Projects are brought forward, growth recovers ahead of the region, and growth-first is the plan from now on. The idle payment system is switched off, and its vendor invoices, politely, for that too.

choices.text: Sign it. Switch it back on.
choices.outcome: The cash goes out within a week, because the system remembered how. The lowest incomes hold steady, your bonus is one month, and nobody writes about a system that worked twice.

steady: A downturn, and your standing jobs-first plan comes out of a folder labelled "Downturn" that nobody has to look for.
Wage support for jobs is renewed for three more Budgets, and firms fill in the same forms, in triplicate, again.
Retrenchment is back in the papers, and your ministry's jobs scheme is back in the Budget, unchanged.
The downturn plan keeps jobs first, announced in last cycle's press release with the year changed.
headline: In a downturn your standing plan pushes growth through it again, and the cranes go up in the west on schedule.
Your growth-first plan is rolled over into the downturn, with a new cover that says "Resilience".
Projects are brought forward again, from a list that has not changed since the last downturn.
Exports fall and your ministry pushes growth anyway, as the standing plan says, reusing the speech about resilience.
lowest: The cash for the lowest incomes goes out again within a week of the Budget, as your standing plan says.
Your standing plan cushions the lowest incomes through another downturn, and again nobody reports on rent paid on time.
The plan for the lowest incomes is renewed through the downturn, and Finance asks once, out of habit, whether it is temporary.
The downturn cash goes out in March under your standing plan, and is spent on rent, school shoes and hawker food.

title: The Indicators, Before an Election
body: A general election is due within the year, and your ministry must settle its plan for the next three Budgets before Nomination Day. The plan sets your National Bonus: three months' salary when the national targets for growth, jobs and incomes are met, up to six when they are beaten. Your branch chairman has sent, unasked, a list of what the ward would like announced.

choices.text: Spread the gains widely before polling day.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The measures land after the indicators are measured, so your bonus is one month. Residents like the measures anyway; the indicators were not voting.

choices.outcome: The measures land in time and are felt in every block, and your bonus is three months. Your branch chairman reads them out at the CCC dinner, from a printout, with feeling.

choices.text: Hold the line on the targets.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The targets are nearly met, for a bonus of two months, and the campaign is a little quieter than your branch would like.

choices.outcome: The targets are met and your bonus is four months. Your branch chairman asks, politely, whether anything at all could be announced, and is sent the targets.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses its target by a tenth of a point, and the formula pays no National Bonus. In an election year, a tenth of a point gets a press conference.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median, and your bonus is three months. The chart is on a campaign flyer by Friday, cropped so the axis starts somewhere encouraging.

variants.body: Your Permanent Secretary is briefing you on the ministry's plan for the next three Budgets, which also sets your National Bonus: three months' salary for meeting the national targets, up to six for beating them. The briefing pauses, politely, at a slide titled "Timing". Everyone in the room knows a general election is due within the year. Nobody has said so for forty minutes.

choices.text: Bring everything forward, before polling day.
choices.outcome: The slide titled "Timing" becomes the whole plan. The measures land in every block in time, your bonus is three months, and your Permanent Secretary minutes the decision with great care.

choices.text: Keep the timing as it was.
choices.outcome: The plan goes ahead on its original schedule, after polling day. The targets are met and your bonus is four months. Your branch learns about the measures from the newspapers, like everyone else.

choices.text: Use the timing for the lowest incomes.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, and your bonus is three months. The 20th-percentile chart rises, and is reprinted on a flyer at a size the economists would not approve.

variants.body: A general election is due, and the party's election committee asks every office holder for "one thing residents can feel by polling day". Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has three versions, each felt by different residents. Whichever you choose also sets your National Bonus: three months' salary for meeting the national targets, up to six for beating them.

choices.text: Give them something everyone can feel.
choices.outcome: Everyone feels it, briefly, and your bonus is three months. The committee puts it on a poster, and at a walkabout a resident tells you she felt it, and would like it again.

choices.text: Give them the targets, met.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for the targets, met, and your bonus is four months. Asked whether you have anything else, you do not, so the committee finds something in another ministry.

choices.text: Give them the lowest incomes, raised.
choices.outcome: The lowest incomes rise, your bonus is three months, and the chart goes on a flyer. Residents who are not on the chart ask what is in it for them. Residents who are on it do not need the flyer.

headline.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
headline.body: A general election is due within the year, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you went for the biggest, most visible numbers, and your branch has reprinted the flyer that boasted about them. Your officials' draft matches the flyer. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget from here on, without coming back to you.

choices.text: Run it as written.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day, in every block, with the flyer, and this is now the standing plan. At a walkabout a resident says it is the same flyer as last time, and she is right.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, the flyers are pulped, and the safe plan is the standing plan from now on. Your branch chairman asks, twice, whether the change could have waited until after polling day.

choices.text: Pull the flyer. Put the lowest incomes first.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, a new flyer is printed with a new chart, and that is the plan from now on. The old flyers are used, unofficially, to wrap kueh at the CCC.

steady.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
steady.body: Polling day is within the year, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you chose the safe plan, and your officials have sent it again, with its annex on timing left blank. Your branch secretary asks, by voice note, what is in it for the ward. Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget without coming back to you.

choices.text: Fill the annex. Bring the visible measures forward.
choices.outcome: The measures land before polling day, and visible measures first is the standing plan now. Your officials redo the annex over a weekend, and Finance asks why a plan that met its targets needs a timing annex at all.

choices.text: Sign it, blank annex and all.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, your bonus is four months, and the safe plan will now renew itself. Your branch secretary sends a second voice note, mostly a sigh, and the campaign leads on the new lifts instead.

choices.text: Fill the annex. The lowest incomes, before polling day.
choices.outcome: Support for the lowest incomes lands before polling day, and that is the standing plan now. Your branch secretary sends a thumbs-up, the first in years, and asks for the chart in three more languages.

lowest.title: The Indicators, Again, Before an Election
lowest.body: Polling day is within the year, and the next three Budgets need a plan. Last time you put the lowest incomes first, and your branch wants that chart on its flyer. Your officials' draft keeps it, under a covering note that calls it "settled policy". Whatever you sign now becomes the standing plan, rolled over every Budget without coming back to you.

choices.text: Unsettle it. Spread the gains wider before polling day.
choices.outcome: The measures reach every block in time, and visible measures first is the standing plan from now on. Your officials refile the "settled policy" note under a heading that no longer applies.

choices.text: Unsettle it. Hold the line on the targets.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, the flyer has nothing new on it, and the safe plan is the standing plan from now on. Your branch chairman reads the covering note aloud at a meeting, slowly, as evidence.

choices.text: Leave it settled.
choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile outgrow the median again, your bonus is three months, and the plan now renews itself. The chart goes on another flyer, and residents who were on it last time say they have seen it.

headline: An election is due, and your standing plan brings the visible measures forward again, with last time's flyer redated.
Polling day approaches, and your ministry's measures are timed to land in every block, as the standing plan says.
Your branch gets its flyer, its measures and its press conference, in the usual order.
An election year, and the plan is rolled forward to land just before Nomination Day.
steady: An election is due, and your standing plan holds the line on the targets again; your branch chairman has stopped asking.
The safe plan rolls into an election year, and your branch learns of it from the newspapers, as usual.
Before polling day your ministry announces nothing new, on schedule.
The targets are kept through another election year, and the campaign leads on lift upgrading instead.
lowest: An election is due, and the 20th-percentile chart goes on the flyer, cropped so the axis starts somewhere encouraging.
Support for the lowest incomes is timed to land before polling day, as your standing plan says.
Your branch prints the lowest-incomes chart again, and residents on it say they did not need the flyer.
The plan for the lowest incomes renews itself in an election year, and a volunteer translates the chart's caption again.

title: The Recruiter
body: A recruiter has found you on LinkedIn, which you did not know you were still on. A bank would like someone who understands how ministries think. The salary is a number you read twice.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your pass stops working on a Friday. On Monday you have a new one, and a view.

choices.text: Mention the offer, lightly, to HR.
choices.outcome: HR notes your "market value" and, for one ranking cycle, takes you more seriously. It is also noted.

choices.text: Decline. You are not finished here.
choices.outcome: You delete the message. Then you un-delete it, read the number again, and delete it.

title: The Consultancy
body: The firm that charged your ministry $1.9 million for a deck would like to hire someone who knows what ministries actually want. You are that person, apparently. The offer letter is on very good paper.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your first engagement is with your old ministry. The slides are beautiful. They say what your minute papers said.

choices.text: Decline, and tell them why.
choices.outcome: They take it well, and quote you in a thought-leadership piece about public-sector talent.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the letter in a drawer.
choices.outcome: The drawer is the top one. You open it more often than you would admit.

title: The Board Seat
body: A conglomerate wants {post.ask} on its board: four meetings a year, and a fee its annual report puts in a footnote. Office holders may not hold company directorships, so saying yes means leaving politics at the next election. The chairman knows this. He asks only whether you might be free "after".

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} At the election a new candidate wins your old seat. The board seat, as promised, has been kept warm.

choices.text: Decline.
choices.outcome: You decline in writing. You later learn that your letter is framed in the chairman's office, as a curiosity.

options.ask: someone who has worked close to Cabinet
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.
options.exit: The Prime Minister asks you to see out the term, and you do.

options.ask: someone who has run part of a ministry
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister you will not stand again.
options.exit: Your portfolio goes to a colleague who has waited for it, politely.

options.ask: someone who has sat in Cabinet
options.leave: Tell the Prime Minister this Cabinet is your last.
options.exit: The reshuffle announcement thanks you in its second paragraph.

variants.body: At a charity dinner, a company chairman you have met twice steers you to the window. His board needs {post.ask}, whenever suits you. Office holders may not sit on company boards, so saying yes means leaving politics. He names the fee quietly, then again, in case you were being polite.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} A new candidate holds your seat at the election. Flowers arrive at your first board meeting, the first of four that year.

choices.text: Thank him, and decline.
choices.outcome: You decline at the window, smiling. He says the offer will keep, and every Chinese New Year a card arrives to show that it is keeping.

variants.body: A search firm writes, on paper thick enough to stand up by itself, about a client's board seat for {post.ask}, from "a date convenient to you". Office holders may not sit on boards, so that date is after you leave politics. The fee is in the second paragraph. The second paragraph is short.

choices.text: {post.leave}
choices.outcome: {post.exit} Your seat passes to a new candidate. The search firm's next letter begins "Dear Director", and is much thinner.

choices.text: Decline, on your own letterhead.
choices.outcome: The search firm replies within the hour to thank you, and files you under "later". The list of people filed under "later" is long, and well looked after.

choices.outcome: {post.exit} At the election your GRC team fields a new face in your ward. The board seat, as promised, has been kept warm.

choices.text: Decline.
choices.outcome: You decline in writing. You later learn that your letter is framed in the chairman's office, as a curiosity.

choices.outcome: {post.exit} Your ward gets a new face at the election, and the team is returned. Flowers arrive at your first board meeting.

choices.outcome: You decline at the window, smiling. He says the offer will keep, and every Chinese New Year a card arrives to show that it is keeping.
